cards.title: Cross-species single-cell atlas of the aging olfactory mucosa reveals cell-type specific senescence linked to neuroepithelial dysfunction and chronic inflammation
cards.abstract: Introduction Aging of the olfactory mucosa is associated with progressive olfactory dysfunction, impaired neuroepithelial regeneration, and persistent inflammation. However, the cellular and molecular mechanism linking age-related changes, cellular senescence, and chronic inflammation in the olfactory epithelium remain unclear. We hypothesized that aging promotes cell-type-specific senescence programs, which contribute to inflammatory remodeling and impaired neuroepithelial homeostasis in the olfactory mucosa. Methods We integrated publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets from young and aged human and mouse olfactory mucosa to characterize age-associated changes in cellular composition and transcriptional states. Cellular senescence was assessed using canonical senescence- associated genes, including CDKN2A/p16, SenMayo gene-signature scoring, and SenePy based cell-type-specific senescence scoring. Differential gene expression, cell-type-specific transcriptional profiles and senescence-associated inflammatory programs were evaluated across age groups and compared between species. Our in-house human chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) scRNA-seq cohort was additionally analyzed to determine whether chronic sinonasal inflammation was associated with amplification of age-related senescence programs. Results Analysis revealed conserved cellular complexity and identified approximately twenty transcriptionally distinct clusters in both species. In older samples, aging was associated with substantial remodeling of cellular composition and increased cell-type-specific senescence signatures across the olfactory mucosa. Senescence-enriched epithelial and stromal populations showed increased expression of senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) programs, including inflammatory cytokines, neutrophil-recruiting chemokines, and inflammasome-related genes. Cross species analysis identified both conserved and species-specific patterns of senescence, with epithelial involvement in humans and greater stromal and immune involvement in mice. Senescence in fibroblasts emerged as a conserved feature across species. Our in-house CRS cohort showed that chronic inflammatory disease was associated with increased enrichment of age-related senescence programs, particularly within epithelial and stromal cells. Discussion We found that cellular senescence in the aging olfactory mucosa follows a consistent pattern across cell types. The data also link inflammatory signaling to chronic inflammation and impaired neuroepithelial homeostasis. The expansion of these programs in CRS suggests that cellular senescence may represent an important mechanistic link between aging, persistent sinonasal inflammation, and olfactory dysfunction, and supports future functional studies to evaluating senescence-targeted approaches aimed at restoring olfactory tissue regeneration.

cards.title: Acetate promotes nutritional adaptation in Escherichia coli
cards.abstract: Escherichia coli often releases acetate in its environment where it can accumulate to concentrations high enough to inhibit the bacterium's own growth. Here, we demonstrate that acetate promotes E. coli adaptation to nutrient changes by accelerating growth resumption, with as little as 250 M acetate being sufficient to shorten the lag phase by several hours. Acetate was found to be consumed via acetyl-CoA synthetase very early after the nutrient change. Transcriptomics, metabolomics and 13C-isotope labeling experiments show that acetate replenishes metabolic pools in the tricarboxylic acid cycle and upper glycolysis. Single-cell analyses reveal that acetate increases the adaptation speed of individual cells switching to the new nutrient. We conclude that the reuse of excreted acetate by E. coli facilitates nutritional adaptation by transiently replenishing central metabolite pools. This work identifies an unexpected role of acetate in the nutritional adaptation of E. coli, providing new insights into the physiological relevance of overflow metabolism.

cards.title: Clinical translation of ultrasoft Fleuron probes for stable, high-density, and bidirectional brain interfaces
cards.abstract: Building brain foundation models to capture the underpinning neural dynamics of human behavior requires large functional neural datasets for training, which current implantable Brain-Computer Interfaces (iBCIs) cannot achieve due to the instability of rigid materials in the brain. How can we realize high-density neural recordings with wide brain region access at single-neuron resolution, while maintaining the long-term stability required? In this study, we present a novel approach to overcome these trade-offs, by introducting Fleuron, a family of ultrasoft, ultra-low-k dielectric materials compatible with thin-film scalable microfabrication techniques. We successfully integrate up to 1,024 sites within a single minimally-invasive Fleuron depth electrode. The combination of the novel implant material and geometry enables single-unit level recordings for 18 months in rodent models, and achieves a large number of units detected per electrode across animals. 128-site Fleuron probes, that cover 8x larger tissue volume than state-of-the-art polyimide counterparts, can track over 100 single-units over months. Stability in neural recordings correlates with reduced glial encapsulation compared to polyimide controls up to 9-month post-implantation. Fleuron probes are integrated with a low-power, mixed-signal ASIC to achieve over 1,000 channels electronic interfaces and can be safely implanted in depth using minimally-invasive surgical techniques via a burr hole approach without requiring specialized robotics. Fleuron probes further create a unique contrast in clinical 3T MRI, allowing for post-operative position confirmation. Large-animal and ex vivo human tissue studies confirm safety and functionality in larger brains. Finally, Fleuron probes are used for the first time ever intraoperatively during planned resection surgeries, confirming in-human usability, and demonstrating the potential of the technology for clincical translation in iBCIs.

cards.title: Statistical tests for bivariate spatial association across multi-omics data with disjoint coordinates
cards.abstract: Spatial biology has entered a new era of multimodal profiling, with multiple, high-dimensional spatial omics types being measured on consecutive tissue slices, or co-assayed on the same slice. Interest then lies in statistical testing for spatial association between the features of the different modalities, to gain insight in biological processes. One major challenge is the multitude of bivariate combinations, leading to high computational demands. Another difficulty is the difference in spatial resolution between technologies, implying no one-to-one matching between the measurement spots of the different modalities, even after alignment. As a result, common statistical measures such as joint distributions and correlations are not defined, and tests need to rely on spatial vicinity only. Moreover, we argue that many existing bivariate association tests address an inappropriate null hypothesis, or make inappropriate assumptions, both implying absence of spatial autocorrelation in any of the features and leading to misleading conclusions. As a remedy, we modify tests for the detection of spatially variable genes (Moran's I, Gaussian processes and generalized additive models) to derive bivariate spatial association tests across modalities with non-overlapping coordinate sets, and provide variance estimators that do account for spatial autocorrelation. We develop inference methods for single sections as well as for replicated experiments with multiple sections, and compare their performance in nonparametric and parametric simulations. Finally, we apply the newly developed methods to two co-assayed spatial transcriptomics and metabolomics datasets from mouse and human. The full suite of tests is available from BioConductor as the R-package sbivar.

cards.title: CortexDecoder: Efficient fMRI-to-Image Reconstruction from Cortical Flatmaps
cards.abstract: Recent brain decoding work has shown the potential of Vision Transformers (ViTs) to learn mappings from neural representations to visual features. Here we present CortexDecoder, a framework that reconstructs viewed images from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) flatmaps, which are neural responses projected onto the cortical surface and unfolded into 2D images. We show that a frozen, pretrained cortical foundation model is sufficient for competitive reconstruction. A frozen CortexMAE encoder turns flatmap patches into brain tokens, and two lightweight cross-attention bridges map these tokens to semantic CLIP embeddings and low-level image features. The final image is generated using a frozen SDXL-unCLIP model which takes a low-level image reconstruction as an initial image and a predicted CLIP embedding used to condition the image generation. On Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) Subject 1 reconstruction benchmarks, CortexDecoder is competitive with prior methods and the best for cortical flatmap methods without multi-subject pretraining. CortexDecoder achieves this performance while training far fewer parameters compared to prior methods.

cards.title: Single-nucleus proteomics reveals proteins regulating LPS-induced nucleocytoplasmic transport in macrophages
cards.abstract: Background Variation in the proteome configuration of unstimulated cells may be associated with differences in how individual cells respond to stimulation. Multiplexed single-cell proteomics by liquid chromatography mass spectrometry can uncover these associations at high depth and throughput. Results Here we develop an approach that links proteomic and phenotypic variation across individual cells and nuclei to identify potential regulators of biological processes for targeted validation. We apply this approach to identify regulators of nucleocytoplasmic protein transport in macrophages stimulated with lipopolysaccharide (LPS). We quantify the proteomes of 3,412 individual nuclei across the dynamic response to LPS and associated proteomic variation with differences in transport. Within minutes of stimulation, protein transport in individual nuclei correlates strongly with the abundance of known protein transport regulators, revealing how natural protein variation relates to cellular responses. Simple biophysical constraints, including nuclear pore abundance, partially explain the variation in LPS-induced nucleocytoplasmic transport. We select 16 new potential regulators of protein transport to test by targeted knockdown. The knockdown phenotypes confirm the inferences derived from natural protein and functional variation of single nuclei. Conclusions By linking proteomic and functional variation among individual nuclei, we identify proteins associated with LPS-induced nucleocytoplasmic transport and prioritize potential regulators for functional validation. This approach should be broadly applicable to discovering protein regulators and enhancing the functional interpretation of single-cell omics data.

cards.title: Concurrent bone-modifying agent use and fracture risk in patients treated with radium-223 for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer: A Japanese claims database study.
cards.abstract: Radium-223 dichloride (Ra-223) prolongs overall survival in castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) with symptomatic bone metastases, but the ERA-223 trial reported an increased fracture rate when Ra-223 was combined with an androgen receptor signaling inhibitor (ARSI), and concurrent use of a bone-modifying agent (BMA) attenuated this risk. Few studies have quantitatively characterized real-world concurrent BMA use during Ra-223 treatment in Asia, or examined its association with fracture risk with competing risks taken into account. This study aimed to describe the real-world rate of concurrent BMA use during Ra-223 treatment in Japan and to quantify its association with fracture risk. In this retrospective observational study using the DeSC Database, a Japanese administrative claims database, 1,132 patients with a claim for Ra-223 were identified, and the date of the first claim was defined as day 0. After excluding patients with less than one year of prior observation, patients with another primary cancer, and patients who had a fracture diagnosis or the competing event of death, or whose observation ended, during the 8 weeks after day 0, the analysis set comprised 538 patients. Concurrent BMA use was defined by a claim for denosumab or zoledronic acid during the 8 weeks after day 0. The primary outcome was any fracture, identified from fracture diagnosis codes recorded after the landmark. Cumulative incidence was estimated with death as a competing event, and multivariable Fine-Gray regression and inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) were applied. Concurrent BMA use was present in 250 patients (46.5%). Any fracture occurred in 91 patients, with a cumulative incidence of 14.1% at 12 months and 19.0% at 24 months after the landmark. Concurrent BMA use was associated with a lower fracture risk (subdistribution hazard ratio [sHR] 0.26, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.16-0.42), whereas concurrent ARSI use (sHR 2.18, 95% CI 1.40-3.40) and a history of fracture diagnosis (sHR 2.55, 95% CI 1.32-4.92) were associated with increased risk. The IPTW analysis was concordant (sHR 0.29, 95% CI 0.18-0.47). Concurrent BMA use during Ra-223 treatment remained below half in Japanese real-world practice, yet was associated with a substantially lower fracture risk under competing risks.

cards.title: Spatial Transcriptomics Reveals Host Gene Expression Patterns Associated with Naegleria fowleri Infection in the Murine Brain
cards.abstract: Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis (PAM), caused by the free-living amoebae Naegleria fowleri, is a devastating disease with a mortality rate exceeding 97%. Despite its severity, the spatial and temporal characteristics of the host immune response to infection within the brain remain poorly understood. Here, we used spatially resolved transcriptomic profiling to characterize region-specific gene expression patterns in brain tissue collected at multiple time points following intranasal inoculation of N. fowleri in mice. Our analysis revealed pronounced pro-inflammatory transcriptional signatures that varied across brain regions and over the course of infection. Cell type-associated gene expression profiles suggested the involvement of several immune cell populations, including macrophages, neutrophils, and natural killer T cells, alongside transcriptional changes associated with neural cell populations. Notably, inflammatory transcriptional signatures also were detected in brain regions without detectable amoebae, indicating that host responses extend beyond regions of apparent parasite localization. Collectively, these findings provide a spatial and temporal characterization of the host transcriptional response during experimental PAM, highlighting inflammatory gene expression signatures and putative immune and neural cell populations associated with disease progression. This study provides a foundation for future investigations into the cellular and molecular processes underlying neuroinflammation during N. fowleri infection.

cards.title: A report-supervised EEG-language foundation model enables broad, interactive clinical interpretation
cards.abstract: Medical AI for complex signals such as electroencephalography (EEG) relies on costly expert annotations and predefined diagnostic labels that fail to capture the richness and nuance of clinical interpretation. Whether models trained on routine clinical reports can overcome these limitations while matching expert-supervised performance remains unclear. We introduce EEG Copilot, a biosignal-language foundation model trained on routine EEG-report pairs without dedicated task-specific expert annotations. Across two external datasets (6,078 EEGs), EEG Copilot performed on par with a state-of-the-art expert-supervised model across 11 shared findings (mean AUROC 0.80-0.81), corroborated by direct neurologist review of 200 EEGs. Beyond predefined diagnostic categories in conventional EEG AI, EEG Copilot assessed 23 clinical characteristics through natural-language questions in English and German across 9,689 EEGs from four hospitals (mean AUROC 0.80-0.82), demonstrating that automated EEG assessment need no longer be confined to fixed diagnostic outputs. Crucially, EEG Copilot generated integrated clinical impressions directly from EEG rather than isolated predictions with shuffled-report controls supporting recording-specific content and neurologist review of 800 impressions showing that most were accurate or clinically usable with minor errors. These findings chart a path beyond label-bound medical AI, transforming routine clinical reports into scalable supervision for flexible, language-driven assessment and integrated interpretation of complex physiological signals.

cards.title: MolMap resolves functional chromatin responses to small-molecule perturbation
cards.abstract: Small molecules can alter chromatin through protein-, DNA- and physicochemical interactions, yet current approaches do not directly resolve where these perturbations produce an immediate functional chromatin response in native nuclear environments. Here we present MolMap (chromatin-small Molecule Mapping), a sequencing-based method that profiles genome-wide chromatin responses to chemically unmodified compounds in isolated, non-crosslinked nuclei. Rather than measuring ligand binding, protein occupancy or downstream gene expression, MolMap identifies genomic regions where small-molecule exposure produces an immediate functional chromatin response. By quantifying changes in Tn5 accessibility and local chromatin organization in native nuclei, MolMap captures locus-specific and dose-dependent effects while separating early chromatin responses from downstream cellular adaptation. Across metabolites, protein-targeting compounds, a DNA-binding drug and a physicochemical chromatin modulator, MolMap resolved compound-specific and mechanistically distinct responses. Comparison with live-cell ATAC-seq showed that MolMap captures early chromatin responses before broader cellular adaptation. In leukemia models, MolMap revealed a coordinated chromatin response in drug-sensitive cells that was strongly attenuated in resistant models. MolMap therefore provides a native framework for bridging the precision of biochemical perturbation assays with the breadth of genome-wide profiling, extending classical chromatin biochemistry into a genomic setting.

cards.title: Growth-law offset and efficient protein synthesis in fast-growing bacteria
cards.abstract: Growth laws refer to simple relationships between various cellular components and the growth rate for exponentially growing bacteria subjected to various environmental and genetic perturbations. The best studied among these is the ribosomal growth law, which refers to a relationship between the ribosome content and the growth rate under different nutrient conditions. This relationship is affine, which means a linear dependence on the growth rate plus a constant offset. This offset, referred to here as the "growth-law offset" and which is substantial in size, has been rationalized in terms of ribosome sequestration and protein degradation effects in the slow growth regime. These effects however cannot account for the sizable offset observed at medium and fast growth, where the efficiency of protein synthesis is predominant. Here, we use a simple effective model of translation to show that efficient protein synthesis in the medium to fast-growth regime does in fact require a substantial growth-law offset, on the order of that observed in Escherichia coli. Our key observation is that efficient protein synthesis requires a nonlinear relationship between non-sequestered ribosomes and growth rate, but in the medium to fast-growth regime this relationship is well approximated by the affine relation in the growth law, with the offset being necessary for the efficient balance between ribosomal and non-ribosomal proteins directly involved in protein synthesis.

cards.title: Persistent DNA damage reprograms the cutaneous microenvironment into a stress-responsive immunometabolic pro-pigmentary niche
cards.abstract: Chronic ultraviolet (UV) exposure induces progressive pigmentary remodeling of the skin, yet how persistent DNA damage influences tissue-level responses remains poorly understood. Xeroderma pigmentosum complementation group C (XP-C), characterized by defective global genome nucleotide excision repair, provides a model to investigate these processes. Here, integrating chronic UVB irradiation of Xpc-deficient mice with spatial transcriptomics, multi-omics profiling, and functional analyses, we identify a coordinated multicellular response associated with persistent hyperpigmentation. UVB-exposed Xpc-deficient skin exhibited increased eumelanin accumulation, altered melanosome organization, enhanced melanosome transfer to keratinocytes, and regional melanocyte expansion. Proteomic, metabolomic, and kinomic analyses revealed coordinated alterations in inflammatory, cytoskeletal, redox, metabolic, and pigmentation-associated programs. Spatial transcriptomics further identified distinct keratinocyte states and inflammatory immune niches enriched in hyperpigmented regions, coinciding with increased melanocyte abundance and DNA damage. These findings suggest that pigmentary remodeling occurs within a spatially organized, stress-responsive immunometabolic tissue environment rather than reflecting melanocyte-intrinsic alterations alone. Analyses of human XP-C skin and XPC-deficient primary human melanocytes revealed overlapping pigmentation-associated, inflammatory, and cytoskeletal alterations, supporting the relevance of these observations to human disease. Together, our findings reveal a previously underappreciated relationship between persistent DNA damage and spatially coordinated multicellular remodeling, providing a framework for understanding how defective genome maintenance is associated with chronic pigmentary changes and altered tissue homeostasis. These findings may also offer insights into the mechanisms underlying common acquired hyperpigmentary disorders.

cards.title: Spatial Transcriptomics Reveals Age-Specific Cancer Hallmark Architecture in Pediatric and Adult Brain Tumors
cards.abstract: Pediatric cancers are fundamentally different from their adult counterparts. Specifically, pediatric cancers carry fewer mutations, interact with developing immune systems, and have active developmental microenvironments. The tumor microenvironment (TME), which includes the surrounding stromal cells, immune cells, blood vessels, and extracellular matrix, plays a crucial role in cancer progression, metastasis, behavior, and treatment response. To better understand the effects of the pediatric tumor microenvironment on tumor gene expression, we acquired spatial transcriptomic data from 17 pediatric brain tumor samples and analyzed it through a Cancer Hallmarks framework. Cancer Hallmarks, as outlined by Hanahan and Weinberg, provide a comprehensive set of 14 biological capabilities that cancers acquire to enable tumor growth and metastasis. We compared the spatial gene expression patterns of the Cancer Hallmarks gene sets between the TME and neoplastic compartments in pediatric brain tumors. Compared with a similar study of adult brain tumors, in which Cancer Hallmark expression patterns clearly separated the TME and neoplastic compartments, we identified three hallmarks ("Deregulating Cellular Energetics," "Senescent Cells," and "Evading Growth Suppressors") whose predominant cellular compartments differed between pediatric and adult tumors. In pediatric samples, these hallmarks were associated primarily with the TME rather than the neoplastic compartment. This shift implicates an age-specific rewiring of the tumor ecosystem. We also provide clear evidence of strong transcriptomic regulation in genes shared by pediatric and adult neoplastic compartments. Finally, we show how measures of spatial autocorrelation may be used to distinguish tumor grade.

cards.title: Repurposing a biosynthetic enzyme for imaging UDP-glucose dynamics in living systems
cards.abstract: Metabolite dynamics remain difficult to visualize in living systems, particularly for nucleotide sugars that link metabolism to glycosylation and signaling. Here we repurpose Helicobacter pylori UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase to develop UGluS, a genetically encoded ratiometric fluorescent sensor for its biosynthetic product, UDP-glucose (UDP-Glc). Circularly permuted GFP insertion and directed evolution yield an approximately 18-fold excitation-ratio response and an apparent dissociation constant of 32.5 M, with preferential responsiveness to UDP-Glc over related metabolites. Live-cell imaging and microplate assays reveal responses to metabolic, genetic and mechanosensitive perturbations in mammalian cells. In zebrafish larvae, UGluS reveals uridine-induced increases in UDP-Glc availability and fin-fold enrichment. In mouse liver slices and skeletal muscle in vivo, insulin- and glucose-induced decreases in UDP-Glc availability accompany increased glycogen content. These findings establish UGluS as a tool for imaging UDP-Glc dynamics across biological scales and extend the use of biosynthetic enzymes as fluorescent sensing scaffolds.

cards.title: Association of intensity-based walking steps and incident falls: a population-based cohort study.
cards.abstract: Falls are the leading cause of morbidity and mortality, yet they are largely preventable. While walking has well-established health benefits, its role in falls remains unclear. We aimed to examine the association between walking and fall risk. Walking steps were defined as purposeful walking steps (≥40 steps/min) and incidental walking steps (<40 steps/min), differentiated by walking intensity. We estimated hazard ratios (HRs) for incident falls using Cox proportional hazards models across the four walking step categories. Risk ratios (RRs) for the number of falls were estimated using Poisson regression. We also estimated the association between walking steps and the risk of incident hip fracture as the secondary outcome. We included 94,422 participants aged 42-78 years from the UK Biobank, with a median follow-up of 6.87 years. We adjusted multivariable models for demographic, lifestyle, and clinical covariates. Compared with the lowest purposeful waking group (≤3999 steps/day), the second (HR = 0.75; 95% confidence interval (CI) = 0.60, 0.92), third (HR = 0.65; 95% CI = 0.52, 0.82), and fourth (HR = 0.68; 95% CI = 0.54, 0.86) group had lower risks of incident falls. Also, the RRs for the second (RR = 0.78; 95% CI = 0.68, 0.90), third (RR = 0.74; 95% CI = 0.64, 0.85), and fourth (RR = 0.72; 95% CI = 0.62, 0.84) group showed similar results. We also observed an inverse association between purposeful walking steps and hip fracture risk, while incidental walking steps showed no significant association. Higher purposeful walking steps were associated with a lower risk of incident falls, number of falls, and incident hip fracture, although residual confounding cannot be ruled out in this observational study. These findings may help inform future step-based recommendations for fall prevention.

cards.title: Statistical significance testing for spatial domain detection in spatial transcriptomics
cards.abstract: In spatial transcriptomics, domain-detection methods group platform-specific spatial measurement units--cells, bins or multicellular spots--into spatial domains for comparing molecular programs, cellular composition and interactions among tissue regions. However, the number of candidate domains detected in the same tissue can vary with user-specified parameters or model-selection criteria. Whether candidate domains should be merged can be framed as a test of a single-domain null hypothesis, under which each gene has constant mean expression across all spatial units in the combined region. However, testing candidate domains on the same gene-expression data used to detect them may induce post-selection bias and yield anti-conservative p-values, increasing the risk of oversegmentation. To address these challenges, we introduce SigDoTS (statistical Significance testing for Domain deTection in Spatial transcriptomics), a hypothesis-testing framework for spatial domain detection. SigDoTS uses hierarchical testing to determine which candidate domains to retain or merge, with adjustment for family-wise error control. It accounts for gene-gene covariance and spatial dependence and computes p-values by rerunning the upstream domain-detection pipeline on datasets simulated under the fitted single-domain null. In simulations, SigDoTS controlled the type I error rate at the root node under the single-domain null and improved recovery of the true spatial domains when multiple domains were present. In human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, SigDoTS retained superficial and deep Layer 6 domains but merged Layer 3 candidate domains across different initial numbers of candidate domains. In ovarian and colorectal cancers, SigDoTS retained epithelial domains with different gene-expression programs and local immune environments, together with immune, stromal and vascular domains.

cards.title: Subcellular Spatial Profiling Unveils Links Between Neuritic Plaques with Selective Tau Vulnerability in Alzheimer's Disease
cards.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) features widespread extracellular amyloid-{beta} plaques but selective intraneuronal tau accumulation in cortical layers II/III and V, while layer IV remains relatively resistant. Here, we combined subcellular spatial transcriptomics with co-registered A{beta} and pTau immunohistochemistry to determine why neurons exposed to comparable plaque-associated pathology differ in somatic pTau accumulation. Plaque-associated neuritic stress occurred similarly across layers, but layer IV neurons showed attenuated pTau accumulation and reduced somatic expression of a shared neurite-soma stress program involving DCTN1, CALM3, NORAD, and PIN1. Trajectory analysis within layers identified tau-vulnerable and resistant neuronal states implicating calcium signaling, retrograde transport, and lysosomal function. Notably, astrocytic APOE-neuronal LRP1 co-expression increased significantly along the pTau-vulnerable trajectory, and APOE {epsilon}4 was associated with stronger coupling of local plaque pathology to pTau-associated molecular programs. These findings reveal neuronal programs and neuron-glia interactions underlying selective tau vulnerability and resistance in AD, highlighting potential tau-targeting therapeutics.

cards.title: BioLT: Streaming Biosignal Modeling
cards.abstract: Clinical biosignals such as ECG, PPG, and EEG are increasingly acquired as hours-long streams from bedside monitors and wearables, yet existing analysis pipelines almost universally operate on isolated short windows of around 10 seconds and cannot process the long, irregular, frequently interrupted signals. We introduce BioLT, a streaming decoder-only framework for long-context biosignal modeling that turns any window-level feature extractor or pretrained biosignal foundation model into a streaming model. BioLT combines (i) a discontinuity-aware encoding that exposes the inter-window elapsed time as an explicit input channel, so that the decoder can learn to model these gaps as clinically meaningful information, and (ii) a fixed-size compressed memory bank supervised with cumulative summary statistics, which keeps both training and inference linear in the recording length while preserving long-range context. We evaluate on CPSC-2021, VitalDB, MC-MED, and CHB-MIT for arrhythmia, sepsis, and seizure detection and for forecasting up to 20 minutes ahead, using domain features and embeddings from six biosignal foundation models. Across 21 dataset-feature settings, BioLT achieves the highest detection AUROC in 15 and the highest 20-minute forecasting AUROC in 13 settings, and shows consistent performance gains over state-of-the-art snapshot foundation-model embeddings. These highlight the importance of modeling how streaming biosignal representations evolve over time, beyond improving window-level representations alone.

cards.title: π-SPECFormer: A Mass Spectrometry-based Foundation Model for Decoding the Dark Proteome
cards.abstract: In mass-spectrometry-based proteomics, a substantial proportion of acquired spectra remain unidentified, concealing a vast reservoir of biological variations commonly termed the "dark proteome", potentially obscuring sequence mutations, non-canonical peptides and post-translational modifications. Existing deep-learning methods largely rely on supervised training with peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs), limiting their ability to learn from the much larger pool of unannotated spectra. Here we introduce {pi}-SPECFormer, a mass-spectrometry foundation model pre-trained on 291 million spectra through a two-stage framework that combines self-supervised and PSMs-guided representation learning. {pi}-SPECFormer transfers effectively to de novo peptide sequencing, spectrum clustering and modification detection, consistently outperforming task-specific baselines. When applied to proteomic profiles from 103 individuals with lung adenocarcinoma, the model identified nine high-confidence mutated peptides, including six that were absent from the reference databases. {pi}-SPECFormer thus enables unbiased decoding of molecular complexity beyond the boundaries of the canonical proteome.

cards.title: Opportunistic Osteoporosis Screening Using CT-Derived Volumetric Bone Mineral Density Reference Curves.
cards.abstract: Computed tomography (CT) scans are a widely available yet underused resource that can be leveraged for opportunistic osteoporosis screening. This study aimed to develop sex- and site-specific reference curves for volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD) to define dual X-ray absorptiometry (DXA)-anchored percentile thresholds for osteoporosis classification, and to evaluate whether these thresholds identified individuals who subsequently sustain a major osteoporotic fracture (MOF). A retrospective cohort of 4,418 clinical CT scans was analyzed, including a subset of 1,088 scans with corresponding DXA imaging within one year. MOF incidence and timing following CT were obtained from linked administrative health data. CT images were segmented with deep learning models to extract the first lumbar vertebra (L1) and femoral neck from which vBMDs were assessed using internal calibration. Sex-specific vBMD centile curves were generated for each region using Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale and Shape. A receiver operating characteristic analysis with the Youden index defined percentile thresholds that aligned with DXA-defined osteoporosis. Clinical relevance was assessed by determining the proportion of participants classified as osteoporotic by the CT-derived percentile thresholds who subsequently sustained a MOF, and by evaluating the association between CT-defined osteoporosis and time to incident fracture using Cox proportional hazards models. The cohort included 2,368 males and 2,050 females. At the vertebral body, 66.3% (n=67) of female and 41.9% (n=26) of male fracture cases had vBMD values below the CT-defined osteoporosis threshold, consistent with osteoporosis. Among these, 44.8% (n=30) of females and 76.9% (n=20) of males had not undergone DXA screening. Individuals classified as osteoporotic based on CT-derived thresholds had up to 2.86 times higher risk of sustaining an MOF across all vertebral sites in both sexes. These findings indicate that CT-derived vBMD percentile thresholds offer clinically meaningful cut-points for opportunistic screening and support their use as a diagnostic flag for further evaluation.

cards.title: Structural Basis for Human Milk Oligosaccharides Recognition by Evolutionarily Dominant Norovirus Genogroup II Genotypes
cards.abstract: Human noroviruses are a major cause of acute gastroenteritis. Human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) contain glycan motifs similar to histo-blood group antigens and may act as soluble decoys that reduce viral attachment. However, the molecular basis of HMO recognition by the P domain of the major capsid protein VP1 of different norovirus genotypes is not fully understood. Here, we combined ligand-based and protein-based NMR experiments with X-ray crystallography to study HMO binding to the P domain of the latent GII.2, dominant GII.4 and emerging GII.17 noroviruses genotypes. Screening of 12 HMOs by STD NMR showed binding of all fucosylated HMOs to GII.4 and GII.17 and none for non-fucosylated HMOs. In contrast, GII.2 showed little or no detectable binding under the same conditions. Seven crystal structures of GII.4 or GII.17 with complexed HMOs supported fucose anchoring via five conserved residues. The remaining sugar moieties formed genotype-specific secondary interactions with an extended, shallow and solvent exposed binding surface whose shape is dictated by divergent surface loops. GII.4 recognition is mainly driven by hydrogen bonds whereas GII.17 relied more strongly on water-mediated interactions. Chemical shift perturbation from NMR titrations (CSP NMR) of GII.4 corroborated the fucose interactions and gave dissociation constants of 20-33 mM, consistent with weak and rapidly exchanging interactions.

cards.title: Physiological Waveform Features Based Aging Clocks Associate with Cardiovascular Disease
cards.abstract: Aging affects the morphology of photoplethysmography (PPG) and arterial blood pressure (ABP) waveforms. Here, we demonstrate that machine learning (ML) models trained on features derived from PPG or ABP waveforms can predict an individual's age. We further investigated whether the discrepancy between predicted and chronological age (Age-Gap) could serve as a measure of cardiovascular health by testing its association with cardiovascular disease (CVD). From a large perioperative dataset of 17,327 surgical patients, high-fidelity PPG and ABP waveforms were analyzed, and over 840 time-, frequency-, and statistical-domain features per cardiac cycle were extracted using a signal-processing-based tool. These features were then used to develop ML-based aging clocks, PPGAge and ABPAge, trained on PPG and ABP features, respectively. For each aging clock, we evaluated five ML models: Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Random Forest, Lasso, and Elastic Net. Individuals were classified as having accelerated, normal, or delayed aging based on their Age-Gap relative to the model-specific mean absolute error (MAE, rounded up to the nearest whole year): accelerated aging was defined as Age-Gap [≥] +MAE, normal aging as -MAE [≤] Age-Gap < +MAE, and delayed aging as Age-Gap < -MAE. LightGBM provided the best age predictions for both aging clocks, with Pearson correlation coefficients (r) of 0.92 and 0.92 and R-squared values of 0.81 and 0.82 for PPGAge and ABPAge, respectively. Moreover, we found that accelerated aging was significantly associated with higher odds of CVD for both aging clocks, PPGAge (odds ratio, 1.87 [95% CI, 1.59-2.21], p<0.001) and ABPAge (odds ratio, 2.28 [95% CI, 1.51-3.43], p<0.001). Additionally, delayed aging was significantly associated with lower odds of CVD for PPGAge (odds ratio, 0.68 [95% CI, 0.58-0.80], p<0.001). Our findings suggest that aging clocks based on high-fidelity PPG or ABP waveform features may serve as novel biomarkers for identifying individuals with higher odds of CVD.

cards.title: A compact motif vocabulary is differentially interpreted across human cell types
cards.abstract: How a common genome generates diverse human cell types may depend less on distinct cis-regulatory vocabularies than on context-dependent use of a shared one. We have developed CNN-CR, an interpretable neural network that learns regulatory motifs while predicting gene expression across 116 human biosamples. Promoter regulation proves highly compressible: dozens of recurrent motif families retain most of the predictive information of much larger cell-type-specific vocabularies and generalize to cellular contexts excluded from their discovery. These motifs are conserved at their binding sites and enriched at fine-mapped regulatory variants. Cellular context acts at two levels: chromatin state gates which motif instances are available for regulatory use, whereas reader identity determines how accessible motifs are interpreted. ChIP-seq data reveal frequent shifts in reader occupancy across cell types, and genome-scale perturbations support corresponding context-dependent reader functions. Thus, regulatory diversity can emerge through differential access to and interpretation of a compact shared DNA vocabulary.

cards.title: Msp300 Links Autophagy to Nuclear Morphodynamics
cards.abstract: Autophagy is a fundamental cellular process that maintains homeostasis and enables adaptation to stress by degrading damaged or superfluous components. While its core machinery is well characterized, the interplay between autophagy and nuclear architecture remains poorly understood. In this study, we identify the LINC complex protein Msp300 as a novel interactor of the autophagy protein Atg8a in Drosophila melanogaster. Msp300 belongs to the KASH (Klarsicht/ANC-1/Syne Homology) domain protein family, known for its role in nuclear positioning through interactions with the cytoskeleton. The KASH domain anchors Msp300 in the outer nuclear membrane, where it pairs with SUN domain proteins across the nuclear envelope to form the LINC complex, a mechanical bridge between the nucleoskeleton and cytoskeleton. Yeast two-hybrid screening revealed an interaction between Atg8a and Msp300 isoforms E and G, mediated by a canonical LC3-interacting region (LIR). Localization studies show Msp300 associates with Atg8a within the cytoplasm and at the nuclear periphery under both basal and elevated autophagy conditions. Functional perturbations through stress assays indicate that this interaction influences event in and around nucleus, establishing a link between autophagy and nuclear architecture. By exploring the role of Msp300 isoforms E and G in shaping not only nuclear organization but potentially endoplasmic reticulum, through autophagy machinery, this study introduces a new dimension to nuclear envelope biology and opens opportunities to explore how steady state homeostasis, stress adaptation and cytoskeletal connectivity are coordinated at the nuclear periphery.

cards.title: Filament assembly confers the mechanical resilience of the IFI16 restrictosome
cards.abstract: Interferon-inducible protein 16 (IFI16) is a mammalian innate immune sensor composed of a filament-forming pyrin domain (PYD) followed by tandem HIN200 domains that bind nucleic acids. First recognized as a major regulator of inflammatory responses against cytosolic double-stranded (ds)DNA, IFI16 filaments have been implicated in several key mechanical processes involving both host and pathogens, including viral replication restriction, latency regulation, replication-stress responses, and DNA-damage responses. Moreover, IFI16 filaments are ultra-stable, a key trait believed to drive its autoantigenicity. Although recent studies reported that IFI16 undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) via disordered linkers and multivalent protein-dsDNA interactions, whether such a metastable entity provides a framework for the mechanical activities of IFI16 remains unknown. Here, we show that PYD-driven filament assembly confers the mechanical stability of IFI16 condensates by compacting DNA into ultra-stable tangles capable of withstanding forces sufficient to induce duplex deformation. By contrast, HIN200-dsDNA complexes are much more sensitive to ionic perturbation, DNA pretension, and mechanical interference. Together, we demonstrate that filament assembly allows IFI16 to act as a mechano-sensitive restrictor.

cards.title: Neuronal and glial transcriptional states vary with proximity to tangle-bearing neurons in the human entorhinal cortex
cards.abstract: More neurons die in Alzheimer's disease than form tangles, and tangle-bearing neurons can persist for decades, so tangles alone cannot explain degeneration. We combined 6,000-plex spatial transcriptomics with PHF1 immunofluorescence (167,176 cells; 9 donors) and imaging mass cytometry (170,195 cells; 62 donors), measuring each cell's distance to the nearest tangle. Tangle-bearing layer 2-3 excitatory neurons were enriched late along a trajectory of increasing microtubule-associated, synaptic and V-ATPase expression, with elevated p62 and K48-ubiquitin. Tangle-free neurons shared more of this state the closer they lay to a tangle, including higher chaperone and autophagy scores, p62 and nuclear size. Nearby glia had higher disease-associated scores, with astrocytes expressing less GFAP. Excitatory, but not inhibitory, neuron loss was greatest in subtypes closest to tangles and cortical depths richest in phosphorylated tau. Selective neuronal vulnerability may reflect not only a neuron's susceptibility to forming a tangle but also where it lies relative to one.

cards.title: A Senescence-Related Signature for Risk Stratification and Predicted Immunotherapy Response in Breast Cancer: Integrative Pathology and Multi-Omics Analysis.
cards.abstract: Cellular senescence exerts context-dependent effects on breast cancer progression and therapeutic response through dynamic interactions with the tumor microenvironment; however, its pathological manifestations, cellular organization, and clinical significance remain incompletely understood. In this study, we integrated whole-slide pathology images, bulk transcriptomic profiles, single-cell ribonucleic acid (RNA) sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and clinical data to systematically characterize senescence-associated features in breast cancer. Quantitative pathology and deep-learning features were extracted from hematoxylin and eosin-stained images, and a senescence-related signature (SRS) was constructed using machine-learning survival models. The SRS effectively stratified patients into distinct prognostic groups and showed consistent performance across the internally divided TCGA-BRCA subsets, with high-SRS patients exhibiting significantly poorer survival. Single-cell analyses revealed that senescence activity was predominantly enriched in epithelial and endothelial cells, whereas fibroblasts acted as major signal-sending populations and mediated enhanced collagen-related communication with tumor cells. Low-SRS tumors displayed greater immune-cell infiltration, higher immune-checkpoint expression, higher immunophenoscores, and more favorable Tumor Immune Dysfunction and Exclusion (TIDE)/immunophenoscore (IPS)-based predicted response profiles, while also exhibiting distinct drug-sensitivity profiles. Integrative pathological, transcriptomic, and spatial analyses further identified STARD10 as a senescence-associated candidate enriched in tumor regions and spatially concordant with senescence-marker expression at the spot level. Functional experiments showed that STARD10 knockdown reduced cellular metabolic activity in CCK-8 assays and suppressed migration and invasion, attenuated senescence-associated β-galactosidase staining and senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP)-related cytokine expression, and suppressed tumor growth in vivo. Collectively, these findings establish an integrated pathology- and multi-omics-derived senescence-related signature for prognostic stratification and characterization of TIDE/IPS-based predicted immunotherapy-response profiles in breast cancer, while identifying STARD10 as a candidate biomarker and a potential target for further mechanistic and therapeutic investigation.

cards.title: Ecological networks balance connectivity with flexibility to perturbations
cards.abstract: Food webs become progressively sparser as species richness increases, yet the number of interactions grows faster than linearly, placing communities between the limiting expectations of constant degree and constant connectance. Similar scaling has also been documented in other interaction networks, but whether they share a common architectural regime, and what general principle could generate it, remain unresolved. Here, we show that 1,533 ecological networks spanning different interaction types broadly converge on an intermediate link--species scaling regime, with an overall exponent of 1.43. We interpret this pattern through a thermodynamic trade-off in which increasing network connectivity enhances signal propagation while reducing the diversity of independent modes contributing to the network's response to perturbations. Optimizing this trade-off yields a scaling exponent of 1.45, closely matching the empirical estimate, while randomly adding or removing interactions generally reduces thermodynamic efficiency in empirical networks. These results support a propagation--response-diversity trade-off as a plausible systems-level principle underlying how ecological network complexity grows with diversity.

cards.title: Stochastic population growth and its implications for mutation dynamics under carrying capacity constraints
cards.abstract: Mathematical models of mutation processes often assume deterministic population growth, although biological populations are continuously subjected to random fluctuations. Here, we extend a model inspired by the classical Luria-Delbruck framework by introducing stochastic perturbations into population growth while assuming a constant mutation rate. Using Ito calculus, we derive an analytical solution for a stochastic logistic growth model with carrying capacity. By comparing the stochastic model with its deterministic counterpart, we demonstrate that random perturbations can substantially influence population variability, particularly as the population approaches its carrying capacity. While deterministic growth levels off, stochastic fluctuations persist and may become increasingly important relative to the underlying growth dynamics. The magnitude of these effects depends on the relationship between population growth and stochastic volatility. We illustrate the model using real life within-host SARS-CoV-2 infection data and discuss its implications. Our findings highlight the importance of accounting for stochastic population dynamics when modelling mutation-related processes in capacity-limited microbial populations.

cards.title: Programmable Biochemical Logic Computation Through Repurposing Natural bZIP Protein Interaction Networks
cards.abstract: Protein dimerization networks can implement biochemical logic, but their practical realization has largely relied on designing or optimizing protein-protein interaction affinities, creating a major barrier to experimental implementation. Here, we ask whether computation can instead be extracted from interaction networks already generated by evolution. We repurpose experimentally characterized basic leucine zipper (bZIP) interactomes from Nematostella vectensis, Ciona intestinalis, and Homo sapiens as programmable biochemical logic substrates while keeping all measured binding affinities fixed. Using mass-action equilibrium modeling coupled with genetic optimization, we identify accessory monomer concentrations and output dimers that reconfigure these natural networks to perform Boolean operations. Unengineered bZIP clusters computed up to 15 of the 16 possible two-input Boolean functions, including nonlinearly separable XOR and XNOR operations, and up to 13 functions within a 17-gate three-input benchmark. Computational versatility depended on network architecture and input selection, revealing design constraints inherent to natural interactomes. Stochastic perturbation analysis further showed that many optimized configurations preserve logic-state separation under substantial concentration variability. Finally, a nondimensional scaling framework provides a route for translating simulated concentration regimes toward cell-free implementation. Together, these results demonstrate computationally that natural protein interaction networks contain latent, evolutionarily encoded computational capacity that can be accessed through concentration tuning rather than de novo protein engineering.

cards.title: SMFnet reveals principles of combinatorial transcription factor assembly
cards.abstract: Combinatorial assembly of transcription factors (TFs) opens chromatin at cis-regulatory elements (cREs) to establish cell-type-specific gene expression. Dissecting the role of individual TFs and their collective function has been limited by the diversity of TF binding-site arrangements across cREs. A single regulatory sequence can support multiple configurations of TF and nucleosome occupancy, raising the possibility that distinct chromatin states reflect different TF assemblies. Predictive models linking regulatory sequence to chromatin accessibility collapse these distinct molecular states into population averages, obscuring how TF assemblies shape accessible chromatin. Here, we introduce SMFNet, a generative diffusion model that predicts distributions of single-molecule chromatin accessibility profiles from DNA sequence, and PRISM, which identifies sequence features associated with individual molecular states. Together, these approaches enable us to systematically associate single molecule chromatin states at cREs with specific TF binding motifs. Experimental perturbation of these motifs redistributes the corresponding states as predicted by SMFNet, supporting their interpretation as TF-dependent configurations underlying chromatin opening. We then use controlled in silico motif screens to systematically dissect individual and combinatorial TF contributions to chromatin opening. Individual TFs show distinct chromatin-opening signatures, differing in accessible-region width and nucleosome-positioning precision even when associated with similar levels of chromatin accessibility. Combining motifs reveals partner- and spacing-dependent effects on chromatin accessibility, TF occupancy and nucleosome positioning. Genetic perturbation of TF binding sites using natural variation at endogenous cRE confirms that TF-specific properties shape chromatin accessibility in vivo. Together, our findings reveal sequence-encoded principles of combinatorial TF assembly during chromatin opening.

cards.title: Sex differences in latent inhibition and their implications for psychotic disorders
cards.abstract: Latent inhibition (LI) refers to the reduced ability to learn or express learning about a stimulus following prior exposure to it without consequence. It has been extensively studied to investigate associative learning and memory as well as the aberrant attribution of salience to irrelevant stimuli in both humans and animals, a process which is thought to underpin hallucinations and delusions in psychosis. Despite sex differences observed in numerous aspects of psychosis, few studies have attempted to characterise sex differences in LI. This systematic review outlines the current evidence of sex differences in LI in both human and rodent studies, showing predominantly inconclusive and conflicting evidence for sex differences. However, the majority of cases in which sex differences were found were in studies that assessed the impact of additional factors on LI such as drug administration, juvenile handling, and oestrous phase, and demonstrated interactions between sex and these additional factors. Hence, there is stronger evidence for sex differences in vulnerability to perturbations in LI. Furthermore, we present data demonstrating sex differences in latent inhibition of contextual fear conditioning and associated gene expression in the hippocampus in rodents, suggesting sex differences in hippocampal processing underpinning latent inhibition at both the behavioural and neurobiological levels. Although there have been relatively few studies demonstrating sex differences in LI identified by the systematic review, the data suggest that in hippocampally dependent forms of LI, sex differences may be more apparent, which may be of relevance in relation to sex differences in the presentation of psychosis.

cards.title: Janusein and EB Cooperate to Enhance Microtubule Plus-end Catastrophe
cards.abstract: Microtubule (MT) plus ends are organized by end-binding (EB) proteins, yet how EB-associated factors modulate the transition from growth to catastrophe remains incompletely understood. Using spatially resolved proximity proteomics, we identified Janusein (ZC2HC1A) as a conserved, poorly characterized MT-associated protein (MAP). At low expression levels, Janusein tracked MT plus ends and reduced EB comet velocity; at higher levels, it redistributed to the MT lattice and was associated with MT bundling and widespread MT loss. Loss of Janusein resulted in spindle defects in human cells. In vitro, Janusein alone facilitated MT elongation through its C-terminal fragment, but promoted MT catastrophe through its N-terminal fragment in the presence of EB proteins. Molecular dynamics simulations and mutational analyses suggest that an N-terminal loop may perturb lateral contacts between adjacent MT protofilaments. Together, these findings identify Janusein as an unconventional MAP that functionally cooperates with EB proteins to promote MT catastrophe.

cards.title: Impact of cardiometabolic and renal phenotypes on the prevalence of type 2 diabetes in the geriatric population of Añisok, Equatorial Guinea: A prospective cohort study (2024-2025).
cards.abstract: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) represents a growing global health challenge, with management increasingly focused on organ protection and mitigating cardiometabolic-renal risk. In sub-Saharan African geriatric populations, the interplay between frailty, hypertension, and obesity presents critical diagnostic and management challenges. This prospective cohort study evaluated the baseline prevalence of T2D and the prospective risk of major adverse clinical outcomes associated with a concomitant high-risk cardiometabolic phenotype among older adults in Añisok, Equatorial Guinea. A total of 1,702 older adults (aged 60-100 years) were enrolled and followed prospectively from July 2024 to December 2025 (median follow-up: 18.6 months). Participants were stratified at baseline into a High Cardiometabolic Risk Cohort (n = 1,500; concomitant presence of obesity [BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2] AND hypertension [BP ≥ 140/90 mmHg or active antihypertensive treatment]) and a Low-Risk / Control Cohort (n = 202; normotensive and BMI < 30 kg/m2). Baseline prevalent T2D, prospective incident T2D (among baseline non-diabetics, n = 612), composite Major Adverse Cardiometabolic and Renal Events (MACRE), acute renal function decline, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), and peripheral vascular complications were evaluated using multivariable Poisson regression with robust variance and logistic regression models. The overall baseline prevalence of T2D across the entire cohort was 64.0% (n = 1,090; 95% CI: 61.7%-66.3%). Among baseline non-diabetic participants (n = 612), the prospective 18-month incidence of T2D was 31.4% (n = 192). Over follow-up, composite MACRE occurred in 17.5% (263/1,500) of the high-risk cohort versus 4.5% (9/202) in the control cohort (adjusted Relative Risk [aRR] = 3.41, 95% CI: 1.75-6.66; p < 0.001). The high-risk phenotype was also independently associated with prospective peripheral vascular necrosis (aRR = 5.82, 95% CI: 1.44-23.51; p = 0.013) and baseline target-organ damage (aOR = 2.18, 95% CI: 1.84-2.58; p < 0.001). The prospective absolute risk difference (ARD) for composite MACRE between primary exposure cohorts was 13.0% (95% CI: 9.8%-16.2%), while the overall cumulative target-organ complication ARD was 18.8% (95% CI: 15.2%-22.4%). In secondary subgroup analysis stratified by baseline prevalent diabetes status, diabetic participants (n = 1,090) accumulated 263 composite MACRE events (24.1%) compared to 9 events (1.5%) in non-diabetic participants (n = 612; ARD = 22.6%, 95% CI: 19.8%-25.4%; p < 0.001). Concomitant obesity and hypertension are independently associated with a significantly higher prevalence of target-organ involvement and prospective risk of cardiorenal and vascular complications in older adults in rural Equatorial Guinea. These findings highlight the need for early multi-organ risk screening in primary care settings across resource-limited central African populations.

cards.title: Evidence generation for diabetes prevention and treatment through the integration of clinical medicine, nutritional epidemiology, and behavioral science.
cards.abstract: Diet and other lifestyle factors are central to diabetes prevention and management. Effective dietary and lifestyle support requires consideration of differences in pathophysiology, food culture, and living circumstances. This narrative review summarizes our research integrating clinical medicine, nutritional epidemiology, and behavioral science, with a particular focus on diet quality. Analyses of large US cohorts showed that higher-quality plant-based diets were associated with lower risks of stroke and mortality. In longitudinal biomarker analyses, increases in healthful plant-based diet scores were associated with favorable changes in high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, whereas increases in unhealthful plant-based diet scores were associated with unfavorable changes in inflammatory biomarkers. Metabolite profiles related to healthful plant-based diets were also associated with lower type 2 diabetes risk. Building on earlier work on adiponectin and type 1 diabetes, our studies in Japan showed that even small weight changes were associated with type 2 diabetes risk, depending on age and baseline body mass index. Visceral fat correlated with ectopic fat, and fast eating and eating late at night were associated with greater pancreatic fat deposition. In older adults, lower sweet taste sensitivity was associated with frailty and poorer mental health-related quality of life. These findings suggest that diet quality and lifestyle should be assessed together with each person's metabolic characteristics and living circumstances. Intervention and implementation studies based on this largely observational evidence are the next step toward individualized diabetes prevention and care.

cards.title: Correlative insights into luteolin regulating the macrophage-p53-CCNB1/CDK1 axis associated with cell-cycle control in hepatocellular carcinoma.
cards.abstract: The polarization of macrophages and the deactivation of oncogenic pathways within the tumor microenvironment are directly linked to the evolution of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), a relatively frequent cancer in the world. Though the exact mechanism is yet unknown, tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) may alter p53 activity by secreting cytokines. In contrast, the (tumor protein p53, p53) signaling pathway is frequently functionally compromised in HCC as a result of mutation or epigenetic silencing. It is yet unknown if the natural substance luteolin restores p53 function by controlling macrophage polarization, despite its multi-targeted anti-tumor potential. To clarify the interventional role of luteolin in the evolution of HCC and to uncover the mechanism by which macrophage polarization influences this process via the p53 signaling pathway. The functions of pivotal genes (Cyclin B1,CCNB1), (Cyclin-dependent kinase 1, CDK1), p53 and macrophage polarization-associated factors (Interleukin 6, IL-6), (tumor necrosis factor-α, TNF-α), (Interleukin 10, IL-10), (Transforming growth factor beta 1, TGF-β1) were experimentally verified in conjunction with bioinformatics analysis (screening of luteolin targets for intersection with HCC differential genes and pivotal genes), transcriptome enrichment analysis, immune infiltration assessment, and single-cell sequencing techniques. 20 hub genes were screened, 5760 HCC differential genes were found, and 104 luteolin action targets were found. According to enrichment analysis, luteolin inhibited HCC via controlling the metabolism of ROS, extracellular matrix catabolism, and cell cycle pathways (p53, cellular senescence). The presence of M2-type TAMs in the tumor core was confirmed by single-cell sequencing, and their secretion of TGF-β and IL-10 led to aberrant activation of CCNB1/CDK1 and cell cycle dysregulation by promoting the ubiquitylation degradation of p53 and inhibiting its nuclear translocation. Luteolin reversed M2-type macrophage polarization, down-regulated IL-10/TGF-β, and was associated with restoration of p53 function via ATM-dependent p53 phosphorylation. This event may induce G2/M-phase arrest and cellular senescence, as well as suppress the activity of the CCNB1/CDK1 complex. Our correlative results suggest that luteolin may reprogram macrophage polarization (inhibiting M2-type and encouraging M1-type), which is associated with relieving IL-10/TGF-β1-mediated suppression of p53 signaling and subsequent inhibition of CCNB1/CDK1-driven cell cycle progression. Nevertheless, the causal direction between macrophage polarization status and p53 function, the primary cellular target of luteolin, protein-level phenotypic validation of macrophage polarization, p53-dependency of CCNB1/CDK1 inhibition, and direct experimental proof for immune escape remain to be fully elucidated. This study highlights the multifaceted impacts of natural medicines in controlling tumor microenvironment and genome stability, and it offers a novel target for combined immune-metabolic therapy of HCC.

cards.title: Comparative Metabolomics and Lipidomics Reveal Selective Fatty Acyl Partitioning and Metabolic Reorganization Associated with Long-Term Cold Adaptation in Euphausia superba
cards.abstract: Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba) inhabits the persistently cold waters of the Southern Ocean, where lipid metabolism supports membrane function and energy storage. Despite extensive characterization of euphausiid lipid classes and bulk fatty acids, fatty acyl organization across lipid pools remains poorly understood. We integrated untargeted metabolomics and lipidomics to compare whole-body biochemical profiles of E. superba and its congener E. triacantha. Metabolomics revealed differences in glycerophospholipid (GP) and glycerolipid (GL) metabolism, together with alterations in pathways associated with nucleotide metabolism, redox regulation, and lipid precursor supply. Lipidomics further revealed selective remodeling at the lipid-class and molecular-species levels rather than a global increase in lipid unsaturation. Relative to E. triacantha, E. superba showed lower relative abundances of multiple lysophospholipid classes and a higher relative abundance of cardiolipin. E. superba also showed higher relative abundances of polyunsaturated glycerophospholipids, whereas a subset of predominantly polyunsaturated triacylglycerol species showed lower relative abundances. C20:5, C22:5, and C22:6 showed higher relative abundances in the GP pool but lower relative abundances in the GL pool of E. superba. Together, these findings place selective fatty acyl partitioning within an integrated metabolic framework associated with long-term cold adaptation in E. superba.

cards.title: The exocyst is an insulin-sensitive regulator of amyloid precursor protein trafficking and amyloid-beta generation in neurons
cards.abstract: Intracellular trafficking of amyloid precursor protein (APP) critically influences amyloidogenic processing, yet the mechanisms regulating this pathway remain incompletely defined. The exocyst is a highly conserved, insulin-responsive, eight-protein Rab effector complex that directs intracellular transport vesicle targeting and docking. We identified APP in a proteomics screen of neuronal cell surface proteins altered following chemical inhibition of exocyst activity. In SH-SY5Y cells expressing an APP mutant that enhances amyloidogenic processing, RNAi-mediated silencing of exocyst subunits significantly decreased sAPP and A{beta} secretion, accompanied by intracellular APP accumulation. High-resolution microscopy revealed APP colocalization with exocyst subunits in the soma and neurites of differentiated SH-SY5Y neurons and primary mouse hippocampal neurons. Live-cell TIRF microscopy demonstrated coordinated movement of fluorescently tagged exocyst and APP proteins. Proximity ligation assays (PLAs) confirmed close (<40nm) APP-EXOC5 association in differentiated SH-SY5Y neurons, primary mouse hippocampal neurons, and histological sections of mouse brain. To examine whether insulin regulates neuronal exocyst activity, as in adipocytes and muscle, we generated SH-SY5Y cells expressing pHluorin-tagged GLUT4. Using this model, we found that chemical inhibition of exocyst activity prevented insulin-stimulated GLUT4 exocytosis to the plasma membrane. Furthermore, PLAs in both primary hippocampal and SH-SY5Y neurons revealed that insulin increased GLUT4-EXOC5 associations while markedly reducing APP-EXOC5 associations. These findings suggest that insulin signaling redirects the exocyst away from APP-positive vesicles towards GLUT-positive vesicles. Together, our data identify the exocyst as a novel insulin-regulated mediator of neuronal APP trafficking and A{beta} secretion.

cards.title: Risk of fragility fractures in individuals with and without HIV infection: a population-based matched case-control study.
cards.abstract: HIV infection increases hip fracture risk, but evidence in Asian populations is limited. In this large nationwide matched cohort study, antiretroviral therapy mitigated overall fracture risk and reduced postoperative mortality despite persistent skeletal concerns. These findings highlight the importance of bone health monitoring and prevention in individuals with HIV infection. Patients with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection are at increased risk of comorbidities, including osteoporosis, which predisposes them to fragility fractures (FFs). Evidence from Asian populations is limited. This study investigated the risk of FFs in an Asian population with and without HIV infection. We conducted a nationwide retrospective matched cohort study using Taiwan's National Health Insurance Research Database. A total of 3994 individuals with HIV infection and 15,976 matched controls were identified (1:4 ratio). Matching variables included age, sex, monthly income, urbanization, liver cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus, renal failure, and hepatitis B and C infection. Fragility fractures were identified using ICD-9-CM codes, and Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The incidence of overall fragility fractures (AFF) was similar between HIV-infected and uninfected individuals (12.9% vs. 11.9%, P = 0.097). However, HIV infection was associated with a significantly higher risk of hip fragility fracture (HFF) (HR 2.22, 95% CI 1.62-3.06, P < 0.001). Risk factors for FFs included age > 50 years, modified Charlson Comorbidity Index ≥ 2, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) mitigated overall fracture risk and was associated with substantially lower postoperative mortality after fracture surgery (9.4% vs. 36.1%). HIV infection was associated with increased hip fracture risk in this Asian population. ART conferred protective effects on overall fracture risk and survival after fracture, underscoring its net clinical benefit despite skeletal concerns. These findings support targeted bone health monitoring and preventive strategies in individuals with HIV in fection.

cards.title: An open-source semi-automated workflow for multi-omics sample extraction
cards.abstract: Multiomics analysis relies on extracting metabolites lipids and proteins from a single sample A widely used method for this is Metabolomics Proteomics and Lipidomics Extraction MPLEx a triphasic chloroform methanol water extraction but it is manually intensive and depends on skilled operators working around a fragile protein layer Here we present OpenMPLEx a semi automated MPLEx workflow for low cost open source Opentrons liquid handlers A minor change in chemistry pellets the protein so that a robot can collect the aqueous and organic phases from above We compared the automated workflow with two manual MPLEx protocols by liquid chromatography mass spectrometry LC MS based proteomics lipidomics and metabolomics The methods were roughly equivalent and measured similar differences between growth media We then scaled the workflow to 96 well plates and tested it on an 80 sample Pseudomonas putida experiment One operator took all 80 samples from cell pellets to LC MS data in a working week with about 3 h of hands on time rather than days at the bench and quantified about 3 900 protein groups All scripts labware definitions and print files are open source so that other laboratories can adapt the workflow

cards.title: Sidetrak: a de novo-designed miniprotein targets the kinesin-1 coiled-coil stalk to inhibit MAP7 binding and disrupt mitochondrial transport
cards.abstract: The coiled-coil domains of cytoskeletal motors contain regulatory surfaces that offer largely unexploited targets for manipulating intracellular transport. The microtubule-associated protein MAP7 promotes kinesin-1 motor activity, binding a coiled-coil surface that overlaps the TPR docking site (TDS), a regulatory interface involved in autoinhibition. Starting from an AlphaFold3 model of this relatively feature-poor surface, we used BoltzGen to design Sidetrak, a 36-amino acid miniprotein that binds kinesin-1 with nanomolar affinity. Binding requires the TDS and is abolished by mutation of the predicted Sidetrak interface, supporting the modelled local geometry of the targeted coiled-coil region. Sidetrak inhibits MAP7 binding, reduces MAP7-dependent kinesin-1 recruitment to microtubules in cells and causes perinuclear redistribution of mitochondria, a kinesin-1 cargo. Sidetrak binds all three kinesin-1 heavy-chain paralogues, and quantitative interaction proteomics revealed selective association with endogenous kinesin-1 complexes and associated cargo adaptors. These findings demonstrate selective disruption of a motor-MAP interaction by a de novo-designed protein and highlight regulatory coiled-coil surfaces as targets for manipulating intracellular transport. Beyond providing a means to manipulate intracellular transport, this work illustrates the potential of de novo protein design to test structural models of protein interfaces and probe endogenous protein networks to uncover underlying cellular mechanisms.

cards.title: A normalization strategy for extreme proteome regulation reveals distinct targets of eIF4A1/2 and their inhibitor silvestrol
cards.abstract: Cells rapidly adjust protein synthesis in response to stress, signalling and drugs, often converging on the cell's translation machinery affecting the synthesis of multiple proteins simultaneously. Nascent proteome analysis, combining pulsed SILAC labelling with enrichment of newly synthesized proteins (NSPs), can measure these changes proteome-wide. However, quantitative proteomics relies on normalization methods that assume most proteins remain unchanged. When protein synthesis shifts globally, this assumption fails: normalization then erases the biological effect, whereas omitting it leads to misinterpretation of data. Since no approach has so far reliably preserved global changes in protein synthesis, we developed labelled protein ratio (LPR) normalization, which uses the ratio of newly synthesized to pre-existing protein in the global proteome as an internal scaling factor. Two SILAC benchmarks showed that this factor is accurate down to a few percent of labelled protein and recovers defined global differences, whereas twelve established normalization methods did not. Applied to cycloheximide treatment, LPR normalization revealed a 57% decrease in synthesis, which median normalization reported as balanced up- and down-regulation with spurious increases in multiple proteins. After depletion of the core translation initiation factor eIF4A1, LPR normalization uncovered a broad translational repression that median normalization largely masked, while eIF4A inhibition with silvestrol showed a divergent pattern, suggesting secondary effects. LPR normalization thus provides a general strategy for quantifying global changes in protein synthesis.

cards.title: Polystyrene microplastic exposure disrupts mitochondrial pathways and nuclear processes in primary intestinal epithelial cells
cards.abstract: Microplastics are pervasive environmental pollutants that pose a growing concern for human health. Oral ingestion is a common route of human microplastic exposure, yet the proteomic response of the gut epithelium to microplastics remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the cellular effects of pristine and artificially digested microplastic exposure in primary rat duodenal epithelial cells using untargeted proteomics. Cells were exposed to pristine or digested 0.5 um polystyrene microplastics at 10 or 100 ug/mL for 72 hours and were then analyzed by tandem liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Proteins that were both significantly different in intensity compared to controls, with a threshold change of 1.3 or greater, were considered to be differentially expressed. This criterion identified 41 differentially expressed proteins after 100 ug/mL pristine MP exposure, with 19 downregulated and 21 upregulated. Following exposure to 100 ug/mL digested MP, only 3 differentially expressed proteins were upregulated and 7 were down regulated, demonstrating the impact of microplastic physicochemistry. FGSEA pathway analysis revealed that 270 Reactome pathways were significantly altered following microplastic exposure in either condition at both concentrations. These pathways contributed to functional domains including protein synthesis, DNA replication, cell cycle control and aerobic respiration. Overall, microplastic exposure was associated with upregulated mitochondrial respiration, and downregulation of nuclear-related processes including DNA synthesis, transcription and cell proliferation. This study provides targets for future investigation (mitochondria and nucleus) and emphasizes the need to consider biological and environmental conditions for in vitro models of microplastic exposure.
