cards.title: Factors Associated With Worse Performance on Oswestry Disability Index in Neurologically Intact Patients Treated for Thoracolumbar Burst Fractures: A Sub-Analysis From a Prospective Multicenter Study.
cards.abstract: Prospective multicenter cohort study (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02827214). This study aims to identify variables that negatively impact Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) scores after treatment of thoracolumbar burst fractures. Prior studies were limited but found that male patients had better ODI scores and that the integrity of the posterior ligamentous complex was significant for post-treatment outcomes. Other studies found that higher preoperative VAS scores, older age, and increased kyphotic angulation were predictive of nonoperative treatment failure. Adult patients were included if they presented with acute, closed TL burst fractures consistent with A3 or A4 within the T10-L2 region. Exclusion criteria included neurological deficits, suspected pathologic processes, or prior spinal surgery. Spearman correlations (SC) were calculated between ODI at 1-year post-treatment and numerous variables, before the development of a multivariable robust linear regression model to identify independent predictors. One hundred ninety-eight patients were included (122 operatively treated). Female sex, treatment in North America, and higher Charlson Comorbidity Index were associated with worse ODI 1 year after treatment. Furthermore, low-energy trauma was associated with worse 1-year ODI compared with high-energy trauma. A longer time from injury to treatment was associated with a worse ODI. As the posterior ligamentous complex (PLC) designation transitioned from "intact" to "injury suspected/indeterminate" to "injured," the average ODI score increased. A higher TLICS score was correlated with worse ODI. Multivariable regression identified ODI at discharge, low-energy trauma, and indeterminate PLC injury as predictors of a worse ODI score at 1-year follow-up. This sub-analysis indicates that several factors can adversely affect ODI following TL burst fracture treatment. Multivariable linear regression identified the severity of ODI score at discharge, low-energy trauma, and indeterminate PLC injury as predictors of a worse ODI score at 1 year postoperatively. Further work is needed to confirm these findings. Level Ⅰ.

cards.title: Osteoporosis management after distal radius fracture in a Korean multicenter cohort: persistent treatment gap and the pitfall of repeat surgery as a surrogate for refracture.
cards.abstract: After a wrist fracture, osteoporosis evaluation and treatment provide an opportunity for secondary fracture prevention. In a Korean multicenter study of surgically treated distal radius fractures, we found that a substantial proportion of patients had no recorded osteoporosis pharmacotherapy and that counting repeat surgeries as refractures can overestimate their frequency, highlighting important clinical and methodological limitations of real-world fracture data. Distal radius fracture (DRF) is an early manifestation of osteoporosis and provides an opportunity for secondary fracture prevention. However, real-world data on post-fracture osteoporosis management remain limited, and the validity of using repeat surgical procedures as a surrogate for refracture in clinical data warehouse (CDW) studies is uncertain. We conducted a retrospective multicenter cohort study of 449 patients aged ≥64 years who underwent surgical treatment for DRF across nine hospitals in Korea (2018-2024). Osteoporosis treatment, bone mineral density (BMD) evaluation, and repeat surgical procedures were extracted from the CDW. Repeat surgeries were reclassified using a procedure code-interval approach. Osteoporosis pharmacotherapy was recorded in 64.8% of patients, with 47.7% having their first recorded prescription after fracture. Among post-fracture initiators, 82.7% had their first recorded prescription within 30 days. Overall, 35.2% had no recorded osteoporosis pharmacotherapy during follow-up. Although BMD examinations were ordered in all patients, structured T-score data were available for only 72 of 891 BMD examination records (8.1%), precluding assessment of treatment eligibility at the individual patient level. Nine patients (2.0%) underwent repeat surgery; after operational reclassification, four events (0.9%) were classified as events consistent with refracture. Simple enumeration of repeat surgery therefore yielded more than twice the number of events classified as consistent with refracture. DRF surgery represents an important opportunity for osteoporosis evaluation and treatment initiation, although a substantial proportion of patients had no recorded pharmacotherapy during follow-up. In CDW-based studies, repeat surgery alone is an unreliable surrogate for refracture, highlighting the need for chart-level validation of database-defined fracture events.

cards.title: Association of Walch glenoid morphology and fracture patterns in proximal humeral fractures.
cards.abstract: Proximal humeral fracture (PHF) assessment focuses on fracture pattern, bone quality, and patient factors, whereas glenoid morphology-central to biomechanics in glenohumeral arthritis and instability-is overlooked. We hypothesized that glenoid morphology consistent with Walch type B (posterior decentring) is independently associated with complex, tuberculum-involving PHFs. This single-centre, retrospective cohort study analysed 919 patients with a PHF and shoulder computed tomography (CT). Two blinded shoulder-subspecialized orthopedic trauma surgeons independently classified all cases; agreement was quantified with Cohen's κ. Fractures were classified by the Neer and AO/OTA systems and glenoid morphology by the Walch classification. The primary outcome-tuberculum involvement (Neer IV/V)-was analysed by multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age at trauma, sex, and osteoarthritis. The cohort comprised 919 patients (72.6% female; median age at trauma 69 years). The Walch distribution in this CT-selected cohort was type A 42.7%, B 54.4%, C 2.7%, and D 0.2%; osteoarthritis was present in 59.5%. Walch agreement was moderate (κ = 0.53), with disagreement concentrated at the A1↔B1 decentring boundary (p < 0.001). Walch type B was independently associated with tuberculum involvement (adjusted OR 2.07, 95% CI 1.56-2.74; adjusted RR 1.30, 95% CI 1.17-1.45; both p < 0.001) and with greater AO/OTA fracture complexity (adjusted ordinal OR 1.60, p < 0.001). Female sex was independently associated with the outcome (adjusted OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.05-1.97, p = 0.023); age and osteoarthritis were not significant. In this CT-selected study population, glenoid morphology consistent with Walch type B was independently associated with complex, tuberculum-involving proximal humeral fractures. The association was statistically robust but clinically modest (AUC 0.62), and Walch type B morphology represented one of several correlates of fracture pattern rather than a standalone predictor. Glenoid morphology may therefore be worth recording during CT and fracture-pattern assessment; these hypothesis-generating findings are not sufficient to modify current treatment algorithms, but support the inclusion of glenoid parameters in future risk models and prospective studies. Level III retrospective cohort study prognostic study.

cards.title: p53 supports healthy aging
cards.abstract: p53 is a master regulator of cellular stress responses that is also implicated in the aging process. Its role in aging is often considered an example of antagonistic pleiotropy (AP), where it acts beneficially as a tumor suppressor early in life, but detrimentally in late life, for example by driving accumulation of stress-associated, pro-inflammatory senescent cells. However, the causal role of p53 in aging is not well-defined, and the AP model has not been definitively tested through loss- of-function studies. Here we show, contrary to the prediction of AP, that p53 promotes healthy aging in mouse liver by suppressing excessive inflammation and maintaining metabolic function. Multimodal RNA, protein, epigenetic and spatial profiling at the single-cell level in aged mouse liver confirmed age-dependent increase in p53 pathway activation. Hepatocyte-specific knockout of p53 in livers of aged mice, but not of young mice, increased inflammation and immune infiltration. Mechanistically, p53 suppressed DNA replication stress and DNA damage, known precursors to inflammatory signaling. In aged hepatocytes, p53 also directly targeted and maintained expression of metabolic genes, and knockout of p53 sensitized aged mice to metabolic stress-induced liver damage. Complementing these loss-of-function data, pharmacological activation of p53 with the small-molecule MDM2 inhibitor HDM201 in aged mice reversed age-associated suppression of metabolic genes, decreased age-associated inflammation and delayed onset of frailty. These results identify p53 activity in aged tissue as protective rather than degenerative. Importantly, this protective function is pharmacologically targetable, potentially for the benefit of healthy aging in humans.

cards.title: N- and T-genes framework for pathway deregulation: Taxonomy, progression, and protection in cancer
cards.abstract: Background. Pathway analysis is widely used to interpret gene expression, but conventional enrichment depends on arbitrary thresholds and does not quantify deregulation magnitude. Recent reformulations based on average log-fold changes remove the threshold but still average over all annotated genes, diluting the signal from the genes that actually drive the normal-to-tumor transition. The N/T framework, which identifies genes with exclusive expression intervals in normal (N) or tumor (T) samples, offers a selective alternative, but it had not been extended to pathway- level quantification, taxonomy, or cross-cancer comparison. Methods. We define effective activation frequencies for Reactome pathways based on N- and T-genes: for each sample and pathway, the effective N (T) frequency is the fraction of annotated N (T) genes active in a normal (tumor) sample. The analysis proceeds in three explicit steps: (i) cohort averages identify the pathways important in each tissue; (ii) averages over hierarchical-clustering groups, ordered by the number of active genes, reveal sequences of pathway activation and deactivation along progression; (iii) a minimum spanning tree (MST) built on pathway-frequency vectors -- independent of the number of active genes -- defines the molecular taxonomy, and branch averages identify subtype-specific programs. We apply the framework to the full set of Reactome pathways in prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD), lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC), and glioblastoma (GBM), analyzing both tumor and normal compartments. Results. In PRAD tumors (n=499), hierarchical clustering identifies four ordered progression groups and the MST resolves six main molecular subtypes comprising 406 tumors (81.4%): B1 (42.1%; MET/NFE2L2/energy metabolism), B2 (13.8%; RAS/apoptosis/telomere), and four smaller subtypes defined by PTEN (B3), DNA repair and lipid metabolism (B4), inflammation and LXR-mediated lipid metabolism (B5), and neuronal development and base excision repair (B6). An eight-gene perfect T panel reproduces the MST subtypes at gene level. Analysis of normal prostatic tissue (n=52) reveals a hierarchy of protection: immune response, apoptosis, and senescence are lost or partially lost early, DNA repair at an intermediate stage, and cell cycle regulation and receptor tyrosine kinase signaling last; an eleven-gene N panel reproduces this hierarchy at gene level. The cross-cancer comparison shows that this architecture is a general property: DNA repair, cell cycle, and RTK protection are maintained in normal tissue across PRAD, LUAD, LIHC, and GBM, while the specific pathways lost in normals and gained in tumors are tissue-specific (MET/NFE2L2 in PRAD; NTRK/LXR/phagosome in LIHC; surfactant/FGFR/glycosylation in LUAD; TP53loss/lipid metabolism/glycosylation in GBM). Taxonomic heterogeneity decreases from PRAD (six subtypes) to LIHC (two) to LUAD and GBM (one dominant program), paralleling an increase in the number of activated T-genes. Conclusions. The framework eliminates dilution by non-nformative genes, quantifies pathway deregulation sample by sample, and unifies tumor taxonomy with a molecular indicator of progression. Its most distinctive contribution is the joint analysis of normal and tumor compartments across cancer types, which links loss of protection in normal tissue to gain of progression programs in tumors and reveals both shared and tissue-specific cancer mechanisms. The method is general and applicable across cancer types, although quantitative results depend on the underlying cohort.

cards.title: Practical evaluation of AI models to forecast a respiratory seasonal epidemic in Canada
cards.abstract: Public health organizations can benefit greatly from infectious disease epidemic forecasting to guide and support interventions and policies that reduce morbidity. However, accurate and reliable epidemic forecasting remains notoriously challenging and is an evolving field in which new scientific advances continue to support forecasting efforts. Computational models that underpin artificial intelligence (AI) models are promising developments that may improve seasonal epidemic forecasting. This study aims to compare the performance of a selection of AI models previously identified as well adapted to epidemic forecasting, including machine learning (XGBoost), deep learning models (Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), Transformer), time-series foundation model (Chronos), and a hybrid model: physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), against statistical models (Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), Prophet) and a compartmental epidemiological model (CEM) in seasonal epidemic forecasting across Canada. The study uses weekly positivity-rate incidence of seasonal influenza A across eight Canadian provinces during the 2025/2026 season as a test case. Each model generated short-term (up to 5 weeks ahead) forecasts independently for each province from October 11, 2025, to March 28, 2026. We evaluated performance using mean absolute error (MAE) for each province. Our results show that AI models, specifically GRU, Transformer, and Chronos models, achieve lower MAE than CEM in four of eight provinces (Alberta, British Columbia, Prince Edward Island, and Saskatchewan). Meanwhile, CEM and ARIMA outperform all AI models in three provinces (Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba) and one province (Nova Scotia), respectively. Furthermore, data pooling strategies that leverage multi-province data for the target virus or multi-virus data within individual provinces greatly improve deep learning models, and Chronos performs well under zero-shot forecasting in British Columbia. In contrast, Prophet always has the highest MAE, and PINN is worse than CEMs. Overall, AI models performed comparably to, or slightly better than, CEMs. However, these modest gains may not offset their lack of interpretability, high computational costs, and reliance on the specialized expertise required for implementation. We therefore conclude that AI models are best as a complement, rather than a replacement, to CEMs, which remain crucial for interpretability and informing decision-making.

cards.title: An apicomplexan-specific foundation model improves prediction of regulatory genomic signals in Plasmodium falciparum
cards.abstract: Genomic foundation models learn transferable sequence representations through self-supervision, yet their practical value is contested. In data-rich mammalian genomes, task-specific models trained from scratch can match or exceed pretrained models on many regulatory prediction tasks. Whether self-supervised pretraining provides an advantage in small, data-sparse genomes has not been directly tested. We address this in the compact, 23Mbp, A/T-rich genome of the malaria parasite, Plasmodium falciparum. We trained a Genomic Pretrained Network (GPN) via masked-nucleotide reconstruction on 455 genome assemblies spanning 76 apicomplexan species. We then fine-tuned the model to predict a variety of epigenomic features in a held-out chromosome, including transcription factor binding sites, chromatin-accessibility, histone modifications, and 10 chromatin states. Pretraining followed by fine tuning improved prediction of most features, with most of the benefit concentrated on datasets with relatively little labeled data (fewer than 3,000 training examples). In contrast, a human-pretrained model transferred poorly, indicating that phylogenetically relevant pretraining, not foundation-model status alone, drives beneficial performance. Self-supervised pretraining on clade-specific assemblies is thus a practical route to data-efficient regulatory modeling in small genomes where training data is scarce.

cards.title: Is the Bitter Lesson coming to genomic prediction? An untuned tabular foundation model matches or beats specialized methods
cards.abstract: Genomic prediction (GP) is dominated by models designed around assumptions about how genetic variation affects phenotypes. Here we asked how well a general-purpose pretrained tabular foundation model called TabPFN-3.5 does with no genetics-specific modeling and no tuning when given marker genotypes directly. We benchmarked TabPFN-3.5 using a published comparison of 18 GP methods on 18 traits in six plant species. Against the published means, TabPFN-3.5 ranked first on 11 of 18 traits and had the best median rank. Because the published benchmark did not identify its test sets, we reran GBLUP, RKHS and elastic-net models on the same splits as TabPFN-3.5. Against the best of these, TabPFN-3.5 was significantly behind on only one trait, spruce wood density, and ahead on 12 of 18, with significant gains on all three soybean traits and rice flowering time. In the soybean panel, which had the largest number of lines, its advantage was clearest. In leave-families-out cross-validation, where models were trained on some soybean families and used to predict lines from other families withheld from training, every model lost accuracy and TabPFN-3.5 performed on par with GBLUP and RKHS. cards.title: STARgrid - an open end-to-end pipeline for Visium HD
cards.abstract: Grid-based spatial transcriptomics quantifies expression by counting reads, assigning them to genes and, from their barcodes, to capture locations on a grid, which is registered to a microscope image. For Visium HD, only the vendor's Space Ranger performs all these steps, and its licences prohibit redistributing it or software derived from it. We present STARgrid, an open-source, end-to-end, agent-ready pipeline from Visium HD FASTQ files and images to count matrices registered to the tissue. Its counts agree closely with Space Ranger's (gene-total correlations at least 0.9989); it runs 2.0-3.4 times faster and counts 1.9-7.6% more molecules. Unlike Space Ranger, STARgrid always assigns each read to the closest-matching barcode, which gives 0.8-1.1% of matched reads a different location, mostly where adjacent-row barcodes overlap, and places another 2.9-4.6%. This choice and settling ties for each molecule from all its reads are the largest source of added molecules. Around nuclei, counts follow a reproducible pattern: more molecules in a ring just around each nucleus, usually with a dip under it. STARgrid registers the image by matching the nuclei to the whole pattern with the correlation ratio, even where the dip is weak or absent. On lung tissue imaged by Xenium on the same section, this places the nuclei where Xenium does or one capture location away. The added molecules behave as signal: they are inside cells almost as often as the others, and bring 15 of 20 abundant cancer genes closer to Xenium on an adjacent section (P = 0.0414).

cards.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted discovery of natural product geroprotectors: target prediction, aging biomarker identification, and drug repurposing.
cards.abstract: Natural products derived from traditional medicines are valuable sources of potential geroprotective compounds; however, their translation into therapeutic candidates is limited by chemical complexity, polypharmacology, limited mechanistic resolution, and lengthy experimental validation. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers an emerging framework for integrating chemical, pharmacological, multi-omics, imaging, and literature derived data to accelerate natural product anti-aging research. This review summarizes recent applications of AI in three interconnected areas: drug repurposing, prediction of aging-related targets and signaling pathways, and identification of biomarkers for biological aging and cellular senescence. AI integrates chemical, molecular, omics, and imaging data to prioritize candidate compounds, predict drug-target interactions, identify synergistic combinations, and reveal mechanisms underlying geroprotection. However, computational predictions should not be interpreted as evidence of efficacy or causality. Data heterogeneity, sampling bias, limited model interpretability, inadequate external validation, and insufficient pharmacokinetic and long-term safety assessment remain major barriers to translation. Future progress will require an iterative framework that combines AI prediction with target engagement studies, senescence models, organoids, animal experiments, and clinical biomarker validation. This integrated strategy may improve the efficiency, reproducibility, and translational potential of natural product geroscience research.

cards.title: Hyoid Bone Fracture in a Patient as a Rare Cause of Persistent Postoperative Dysphagia Following Anterior Cervical Discectomy and Fusion.
cards.abstract: BACKGROUND Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) is widely used to treat cervical spondylosis, disc herniation, and degenerative disc disease that can cause neck pain, spinal stenosis, radiculopathy, and myelopathy. Dysphagia is a common complication following ACDF. In most cases this symptom is fleeting and resolves within weeks to months of surgery. However, severe and persistent cases of dysphagia do occur, and when they occur, they are rarely attributed to a hyoid fracture. CASE REPORT We report the case of a 76-year-old woman who developed severe, persistent dysphagia and progressive odynophagia following a C3-5 ACDF. Despite initial treatment with oral steroids and a modified liquid diet, her symptoms worsened. By postoperative day 14 she could not swallow, had lost 4.5 kg in weight, and had a persistent cough. A computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a nondisplaced hyoid fracture. She required inpatient admission for IV hydration, steroids, and swallow therapy education. A percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube was recommended, but the patient declined. Her swallowing gradually improved with conservative management. By 10 weeks postoperatively, she demonstrated mild dysphagia on barium swallow, and at 5 months she had complete resolution of symptoms, with confirmed radiographic fusion. CONCLUSIONS Although dysphagia is common after ACDF, hyoid bone fracture is a rare but clinically important potential contributor to severe and persistent symptoms. A hyoid fracture should be considered in the differential diagnosis when dysphagia worsens or does not improve with standard therapy. CT imaging is essential to establish the diagnosis and guide management.

cards.title: Shared experimental materials inflate and reorder cross-participant decoding benchmarks
cards.abstract: Decoding mental states from brain activity underpins brain-computer interfaces and cognitive neuroscience. Decoders are judged by how well they generalize to people left out of training, taken as evidence that they capture what transfers between brains. However, most benchmarks present the same experimental materials to every participant, so held-out participants are tested on materials the model has already seen. Here we show, across 15 EEG, fMRI and eye-tracking datasets and 318 matched comparisons, that shared materials inflate cross-participant accuracy by up to 46 percentage points. They also reorder methods, reversing the advantage of foundation models over handcrafted features on the largest emotion EEG benchmark. The inflation tracks cross-participant item identifiability and, in sealed prospective tests, vanished where items could not be identified. Adding training items improved new-material accuracy more reliably than adding participants. These findings call for reporting new-material accuracy alongside conventional scores and for measuring item identifiability first.

cards.title: mRNABench: A curated benchmark for mature mRNA property and function prediction
cards.abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) is central to gene expression, and its half-life, localization, and translation efficiency drive phenotypic diversity in eukaryotic cells. While supervised learning has been used to study the mRNA regulatory code, self-supervised foundation models support a wider range of transfer learning tasks. However, the dearth of standardized benchmarks limits efforts to pinpoint the strengths of various models. Here, we present mRNABench, a benchmarking suite for mature mRNA biology, focused on human transcripts, that evaluates the representational quality of mature mRNA embeddings from self-supervised nucleotide foundation models. We curate 13 datasets and 81 prediction tasks that broadly capture salient properties of mature mRNA, and assess the performance of 29 families of nucleotide foundation models for a total of 750k experiments. Using these experiments, we study parameter scaling, correlations between sequence compressibility and performance, data-splitting strategies, and the effects of self-supervised training objective on mRNA property prediction. mRNABench can be found at: https://github.com/morrislab/mRNABench.

cards.title: Preoperative SASP burden predicts perioperative vulnerability in older patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery: a prospective cohort study.
cards.abstract: Cellular senescence and its associated secretory phenotype (SASP) represent a fundamental mechanism of biological aging. SASP-related inflammation has been implicated in cardiovascular disease. However, its role in perioperative risk in cardiac surgery remains largely unexplored, and established risk scores such as EuroSCORE II and the STS Score do not regard biological aging or senescence. In this prospective single-center cohort study, 131 patients aged ≥ 65 years undergoing elective cardiac surgery were enrolled. A panel of 19 preoperative SASP biomarkers was quantified by a multiplex immunoassay. Of those, 17 markers were evaluated as predictors of a composite adverse outcome, an adapted multimorbidity score with 21.4% event rate, with MACCE (36.6%) as a secondary endpoint. Logistic regression, false discovery rate correction, bootstrap validation, and incremental value analyses (DeLong test, IDI, NRI) were used. Five markers showed nominal univariable significance (IGFBP-1, GDF-15, TNF-RI, TNF-α, and IGFBP-4), though none survived FDR correction. Adjusted for procedure type, IGFBP-1 (OR = 1.675, 95% CI = 1.175-2.389, p = 0.004) and IGFBP-4 (OR = 1.432, 95% CI = 1.044-1.966, p = 0.026) emerged as independent predictors of the composite adverse outcome (Model M3, AUCcorrected = 0.746), numerically comparable to EuroSCORE II (AUC = 0.727). Model M3 improved net reclassification over EuroSCORE II (NRI + 0.528, p = 0.008) and the STS Score (NRI + 0.418, p = 0.040), with consistent estimates under Firth-penalized sensitivity analysis. Preoperative SASP biomarkers, particularly IGFBP-1 and IGFBP-4, independently predict adverse outcomes, namely multimorbidity, after elective cardiac surgery. They improve individual risk stratification beyond standard clinical scores in older patients, suggesting a measurable dimension of perioperative vulnerability that warrants external validation in larger cohorts.

cards.title: Ulnar styloid osteolysis following distal radius fracture without ulnar fracture: frequency and associated factors.
cards.abstract: To determine the frequency and characteristics of ulnar styloid osteolysis after distal radius fracture without concomitant ulnar fracture. Secondary objectives were to assess associated risk factors and surgical outcomes. A retrospective observational, single-center, radiographic cohort of adult patients diagnosed with distal radius fracture between July 1, 2018, and June 30, 2020, was reviewed. Ulnar styloid osteolysis was documented using wrist radiographs at diagnosis and follow-up. Patients with ulnar fractures or erosive arthropathy were excluded. Time to detection, size, morphology, location, and evolution of ulnar styloid osteolysis were recorded. Associations with patient and fracture characteristics were evaluated using Cox models. 143 patients (104 female, mean age 55.8 ± 17.6 years) were included. Ulnar styloid osteolysis was identified in 16.8% of patients (n = 24), with a median detection time of 56 days (range 24-386). Osteolysis was more likely in fractures with: comminution (83.3% vs. 59.7%, HR = 3.457 [1.145-9.845], p = 0.027), diastasis (33.3% vs. 10.1%, HR = 3.905 [1.646-9.266], p = 0.002), dorsal angulation (79.2% vs. 24.4%, HR 4.766 [1.619-14.035], p < 0.001), impaction (66.7% vs. 17.6%, HR = 5.823 [2.486-15.647], p < 0.001) and active smoking (35.5% vs. 16.5%, HR = 2.650 [1.054-6.665], p = 0.038). Osteolysis was more frequently observed in patients who underwent surgery (50.0% vs. 20.2%, HR 2.541 [1.119-5.770], p = 0.026). No significant association with age, sex, osteoporosis, scapholunate dissociation, step-off deformity, or intra-articular extension. Ulnar styloid osteolysis was observed in approximately one in six patients with distal radius fractures in this cohort; this finding was associated with multiple markers of fracture severity. Question How often does ulnar styloid osteolysis occur after a distal radius fracture without ulnar involvement, and what clinical factors are associated with its development? Findings Ulnar styloid osteolysis develops in up to 16.8% of patients with radial fractures not associated with ulnar fracture in our population. Clinical relevance Ulnar styloid osteolysis after radial fracture occurs more frequently in patients with greater fracture comminution, dorsal angulation, diastasis, and impaction, as well as smokers. It must be differentiated from inflammatory arthropathies to avoid unnecessary investigations.

cards.title: RPFace: From biased structural benchmarks to generalizable RNA-protein interface prediction
cards.abstract: Modeling protein-RNA complexes with co-folding and docking methods is routine, yet these methods are evaluated on benchmarks whose composition mirrors the deposited structures on which they were trained or tuned, leaving open whether their reported performance reflects true generalization. Here, we focus the evaluation on the region that carries the biological signal: the binding interface. For the first time, we construct and release a fair benchmark that stratifies protein-RNA data into distinct structural and experimental groups, providing a more stringent test of generalization than aggregate averages. On this benchmark, we find that accuracy of detecting the binding site using co-folding methods is concentrated in ribosomal complexes and varies systematically with factors such as experimental modality. For docking methods, it is reliable only when the input conformations are already close to the bound state, and it is inconsistent across RNA classes. Both families of methods fail to transfer to in vivo CLIP experiments. To address this gap, we introduce RPFace, to the best of our knowledge the first model that jointly predicts the binding preference of every protein residue and every RNA nucleotide directly from sequence, requiring no experimental structure, template, or multiple sequence alignment. RPFace combines an ensemble of predicted secondary structures with a multi-modal embedding-enrichment scheme that fuses representations from RNA foundation models and structure prediction models. Unlike existing approaches, it is a very small and fast model that delivers stable performance across structural and experimental conditions, is robust to conformational change, and generalizes to in vivo datasets without extensive pretraining. As a result, RPFace matches the state-of-the-art methods on protein interfaces with no evolutionary information, and outperforms them on RNA interfaces, with the largest gains in zero-shot settings despite using only sequence information. The model, code, and data are available at Github.

cards.title: Traumatic brain injury enhances fracture healing by upregulating VNN1 to activate the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway.
cards.abstract: Delayed fracture healing is a significant clinical challenge. Patients with concurrent traumatic brain injury (TBI) exhibit accelerated fracture healing; however, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study aimed to identify key genes and molecular pathways that mediate enhanced fracture healing in patients with TBI. Transcriptome sequencing was performed to identify differentially expressed genes in the peripheral blood of patients with simple fractures and those with fractures accompanied by TBI. Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR), western blotting analysis, micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) scanning, and histological examinations were performed on a rat model of fracture with concomitant TBI. The role of vanin-1(VNN1) in fracture healing was assessed together with its relationship with the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that VNN1 was significantly upregulated in patients with combined fracture and TBI. In animal models, VNN1 expression peaked early after injury and remained elevated over time. VNN1 knockdown markedly inhibited TBI-induced accelerated fracture healing, reduced callus maturity, and downregulated the expression of osteogenesis-related proteins (Runx2, OCN, OPN, COL1A1). Mechanistically, VNN1 activated the Wnt/β-catenin signaling via a non-canonical pathway, manifested by upregulation of β-catenin, Wnt1, and their downstream target genes, along with increased GSK3β phosphorylation. Inhibition of this pathway reversed the TBI-induced healing effect. VNN1 is a key factor mediating TBI-induced fracture healing by non-canonically regulating the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway to promote osteogenic differentiation and bone tissue maturation. This study provides a novel mechanism for understanding the effects of systemic trauma on local bone repair and offers potential molecular targets for fracture treatment.

cards.title: Rethinking endpoints for anti-obesity pharmacotherapy in patients with hr+ early breast cancer receiving endocrine therapy: from body weight and BMI to body composition.
cards.abstract: Body weight (BW) and body mass index (BMI) are commonly used to assess obesity and response to weight-management interventions in patients with hormone receptor-positive (HR+) early breast cancer (eBC) receiving endocrine therapy. However, these measures do not adequately reflect changes in fat mass, visceral adiposity, lean mass and sarcopenia-related phenotypes. This focused narrative review examines whether BW and BMI are sufficient endpoints for evaluating obesity management and anti-obesity pharmacotherapy in patients with HR+ eBC receiving endocrine therapy. PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched for relevant evidence until 23 June 2026, including BC-specific studies of obesity pharmacotherapy and registered interventional trials. Studies have reported increases in total and visceral fat mass after adjuvant BC treatment, while changes in lean mass have been less consistent. The identified BC-specific studies remain mainly retrospective and weight-centric, with none assessing body composition as a key outcome. BW and BMI may be useful entry and monitoring variables, but insufficient as stand-alone endpoints. Body composition should be considered as a complementary endpoint, alongside metabolic, functional and oncologic outcomes. Future studies should also assess endocrine therapy adherence and persistence to better characterize the benefits and risks of anti-obesity pharmacotherapy in patients with HR+ eBC.

cards.title: OncoSpot enables benchmarking of cancer spatial transcriptomics methods across tumor evolutionary modes
cards.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) is increasingly used to map clonal architecture within tumors, yet methods for analyzing cancer ST data are difficult to evaluate because real tumors lack ground truth for copy-number alterations (CNAs), subclonal identity, and malignant cell fraction. Existing ST simulators model normal tissue and do not represent tumor evolution, CNA-driven expression, or the spatial organization of malignant subclones. We present OncoSpot, a cancer-aware simulator of Visium-like spot-based ST data. OncoSpot combines a spatial evolutionary scaffold from DEMON, CNAs generated along the resulting clonal phylogeny with CNAsim, cancer-type-specific malignant transcriptional programs, and spatially clustered nonmalignant cell types, and aggregates cells into spots with known malignant fraction, subclone, and copy-number profiles. We demonstrate OncoSpot on high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, colorectal cancer, and hepatocellular carcinoma, which represent three distinct modes of tumor evolution. Simulated subclones were spatially clustered and showed stronger phylogeny-space concordance than those generated by scCube under matched subclone populations. Benchmarking CopyKAT, CancerFinder, Clonalscope, and RCTD revealed cancer-dependent performance: Clonalscope recovered copy-number signals more accurately in ovarian and colorectal cancer, whereas CopyKAT performed better in hepatocellular carcinoma, reflecting both the assumptions of each method and the copy-number landscapes of the three cancers. OncoSpot's ground truth also exposed a failure mode in Clonalscope's malignant spot identification, in which tumor and normal labels were inverted, and allowed us to trace its cause. These method-dependent behaviors would be difficult to detect in real data. OncoSpot provides a framework for benchmarking CNA inference, subclone detection, malignant spot identification, and normal spot deconvolution, and its modular design and guidelines allow extension to additional cancer types. OncoSpot is freely available at https://github.com/compbio-mallory/OncoSpot.

cards.title: Single-probe, high-yield spatial mapping of diverse short RNA motifs
cards.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics has revolutionized our understanding of RNA biology. Hybridization-based methods map mRNA transcripts by tiling multiple labeled probes along each molecule to generate a visible fluorescent signal, restricting applicability to long transcripts. Short RNA motifs, consequently, can only accommodate a single probe and remain a spatially invisible dimension of RNA biology. Here we present SMOOTHY-FISH, a single probe strategy that directly visualizes short RNA motifs at the single-molecule resolution. By optimizing probe brightness, binding specificity, and target accessibility, our single ~20-nucleotide probe reached the practical ceiling of hybridization-based detection. We quantitatively mapped previously inaccessible short motifs - splice-isoform junctions, individual microRNAs, and structural conformations - in single cells and mouse brain tissues, each validated against orthogonal methods. This unveiled biological phenomena that were previously unknown: ratios of alternatively spliced isoforms are tightly regulated across cell populations, subcellular miRNA fractions are precisely maintained, and a designed RNA structure was found to have a prominent alternative conformation. These findings demonstrate that short RNA motifs possess key spatial information that has yet to be discovered. With SMOOTHY-FISH's optimized single probe technique, short RNA motifs are converted into a new routinely measurable axis of spatial transcriptomics.

cards.title: Before the break: a near-term osteoporotic fracture risk score from opportunistic CT (RAVEN).
cards.abstract: Existing fracture-prediction tools primarily estimate long-term fracture probability and may have limited utility for identifying patients at high near-term risk. Opportunistic computed tomography (CT) provides routinely available Hounsfield unit (HU) attenuation measurements associated with bone mineral density and fracture risk. We aimed to develop and evaluate an exploratory risk-stratification score for first documented subsequent fragility fracture over 1-3 years. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 240 consecutive patients identified through a dedicated osteoporosis clinic between 2021 and 2023. Time to event was calculated from the index CT to the first documented subsequent fragility-fracture episode. Patients without a subsequent fracture were censored at their last osteoporosis-clinic or imaging assessment documenting no new fracture. Multiple fractures arising from the same fall or first fracture episode were counted as one patient-level event. RAVEN (Radiodensity, Age, Vertebral fracture history, Extravertebral fracture history, Nottingham) was derived using subsequent fracture occurrence during observed follow-up as the original binary outcome. The completed score was subsequently evaluated for time to first documented subsequent fracture using Cox regression, Kaplan-Meier estimates, Harrell's C-index, time-dependent AUC and IPCW Brier scores. During 760.1 person-years at risk, 91/240 patients (37.9%) sustained a first documented subsequent fragility fracture. Each one-point increase in RAVEN was associated with a higher fracture hazard (HR 1.14, 95% CI 1.08-1.20; p < 0.001), with no evidence of non-proportional hazards (p = 0.188). Harrell's C-index was 0.636 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.564-0.709). Kaplan-Meier curves differed significantly across RAVEN categories (log-rank p < 0.001). Estimated cumulative fracture risks at 1, 2 and 3 years were 6.8%, 9.7% and 9.7% for scores < 4; 9.9%, 24.3% and 32.5% for scores 4-11; and 32.0%, 41.7% and 47.5% for scores ≥ 12. Time-dependent AUCs at these horizons were 0.636, 0.620 and 0.642, respectively. RAVEN demonstrated graded stratification of time to first documented subsequent fragility fracture using opportunistic CT attenuation measurements and clinical variables. These findings support its potential for 1- to 3-year fracture-risk stratification, although external validation and prospective clinical-impact assessment are required before clinical use.

cards.title: Quantifying subcellular organization from localization to co-occurrence with InSpace
cards.abstract: Cell identity and function depend not only on molecular abundance, but also on how molecules are organized within cells. Although spatial transcriptomics now resolves individual RNA molecules within cells, routine computational workflows reduce these measurements to cell-by-gene count matrices, retaining abundance while discarding information about intracellular localization and molecular co-occurrence. This loss of spatial information creates a need for scalable methods that preserve subcellular detail and enable comparisons across diverse cellular morphologies. Therefore, we present InSpace, a scalable framework for quantifying these complementary dimensions of subcellular organization. InSpace-R maps transcripts onto a continuous radial coordinate anchored to nuclear and cell boundaries, while InSpace-C measures distance-dependent co-occurrence or depletion of molecular pairs. Simulations and orthogonal biochemical references support accurate measurements, with scalability demonstrated on datasets containing 275 million transcripts. RNA-RNA and RNA-DNA analyses recover organelle-linked neighbourhoods and associations between nascent transcripts and their genomic origins. Analysis of B and plasma cells across 58 tumour datasets spanning 12 cancer types reveals that reduced MHC-II transcript abundance accompanies more peripheral localization and stronger mutual co-occurrence, separating these transcripts from a program enriched for ER-targeted proteins. InSpace makes intracellular organization accessible alongside abundance, enabling discovery of spatial programs that distinguish cellular states and generate hypotheses about their functional specialization.

cards.title: Is Undiagnosed Dysglycemia Common in Orthopaedic Surgery and Is it Associated With 30-day Outcomes? A Large-database Study.
cards.abstract: Given that patients undergoing orthopaedic surgery frequently share risk factors that are associated with metabolic syndrome, the patients orthopaedic surgeons treat may be especially likely to have undiagnosed dysglycemia. Although its broader impact is documented in other specialties, its specific prevalence and association with postoperative outcomes after orthopaedic procedures remains incompletely defined. Quantifying this hidden burden is important to developing individual risk profiles, refining perioperative decision-making, and establishing targeted preoperative medical management strategies for patients considering orthopaedic surgery. In a large-database study, we asked: (1) In adults who underwent orthopaedic surgery, what proportion of patients had previously undiagnosed dysglycemia? (2) Was undiagnosed dysglycemia associated with increased odds of 30-day readmission and reoperation compared with patients with normoglycemia? (3) What was the relationship between preoperative HbA1c levels and the 30-day risk of complications in patients who underwent orthopaedic surgery? Among the 2,990,063 procedures recorded in the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program database (2021-2023), 25% (735,259 of 2,990,063) were orthopaedic. After excluding 75% (2,254,804 of 2,990,063) of nonorthopaedic procedures and 16% (493,272 of 2,990,063) of orthopaedic procedures without documented preoperative HbA1c, 8% (241,987 of 2,990,063) of all procedures were analyzed. Patients were assigned to one of eight glycemic groups (normoglycemic, undiagnosed prediabetes, undiagnosed diabetes, or diagnosed diabetes with near-normal, very good, good, poor, and very poor glycemic control) based on diabetes diagnosis and HbA1c level. The study cohort included patients undergoing a range of procedures, primarily consisting of total joint arthroplasty, fracture fixation, and spine surgery. The mean ± SD patient age was 66 ± 12 years and 56% [134,741 of 241,987] of patients were female. To address the first research question, the percentage of patients with previously undiagnosed dysglycemia in each cohort was measured, supplemented by a best-case sensitivity analysis to provide a conservative estimate for the entire surgical population. The second and third research questions investigated the association of undiagnosed dysglycemia on 30-day odds of readmission and reoperation and the relationship between preoperative HbA1c and 30-day odds of complications, using multivariable logistic regression adjusted for demographic, comorbidity, and procedural factors. To illustrate variation across operations, the 30-day complication rate of patients across HbA1c strata was evaluated for the 10 most frequent primary Current Procedural Terminology-coded procedures. We found that 22% (52,609 of 241,987) of patients with a recorded preoperative HbA1c had undiagnosed prediabetes and 4% (10,690 of 241,987) of patients met the criteria for undiagnosed diabetes. In a best-case sensitivity analysis in which we assumed that all patients without an HbA1c measurement did not have diabetes and had normoglycemia, the smallest percentage of patients with previously undiagnosed dysglycemia would have been 9% (63,299) across all 735,259 patients who underwent orthopaedic surgery. After adjusting for potentially confounding variables, neither prediabetes nor diabetes was independently associated with increased odds of 30-day readmission (adjusted OR 0.95 [95% CI 0.88 to 1.0]; p = 0.12 and adjusted OR 0.99 [95% CI 0.84 to 1.2]; p = 0.94) or reoperation (adjusted OR 0.94 [95% CI 0.85 to 1.0]; p = 0.25 and adjusted OR 0.99 [95% CI 0.84 to 1.2]; p = 0.94) compared with patients with normoglycemia. The adjusted ORs for any 30-day complication were higher in patients with undiagnosed diabetes (adjusted OR 1.1 [95% CI 1.0 to 1.2]; p = 0.03) and increased across HbA1c strata in those with diagnosed diabetes (adjusted OR 1.2, 1.1, 1.2, 1.4, and 2.0; all p ≤ 0.009) compared with patients with normoglycemia. Procedure-level analyses showed consistent patterns with variable magnitude: 30-day rates of any complication in THA rose from 5% (1425 of 27,812) to 17% (49 of 294) across HbA1c strata, whereas 30-day complication rates peaked at 30% (203 of 675) in hinged TKA and at 22% (11 of 49) in revision TKA. On the other hand, 30-day complication rates in shoulder procedures and knee arthroscopy remained uniformly low (< 6%) with minimal variation by HbA1c. Unrecognized dysglycemia is common among patients undergoing orthopaedic surgery and is associated with postoperative morbidity. Selective preoperative HbA1c assessment and procedure-specific targets may improve perioperative risk stratification. Examining these effects in clinical studies with procedure-specific preoperative HbA1c screening to identify and appropriately treat patients at risk could help to further validate these findings. Level III, therapeutic study.

cards.title: American Indian and Alaska Native Patients Undergoing Hip Fracture Surgery: A National Retrospective Cohort Study Between 2016 and 2022.
cards.abstract: Racial and ethnic disparities have been reported in the treatment of hip fractures; however, American Indian and Alaska Native (AI/AN) patients are often excluded. No existing racial disparity studies have evaluated the management and outcomes of hip fractures among AI/AN patients. We aim to assess whether there are disparities in risk factors, management, and complications in the surgical treatment of hip fractures among AI/AN patients. This retrospective cohort study used the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (NSQIP) database to analyze AI/AN and White patients undergoing surgical treatment of hip fractures between 2016 and 2022. Descriptive statistics, t-tests, chi-squared tests, and multiple regression models were used to assess differences in patient demographics, preoperative comorbidities, time to surgery (TTS), and postoperative complications. AI/AN patients were significantly younger than White patients yet had higher rates of preoperative comorbidities (diabetes [P < 0.001], smoking [P < 0.001], dialysis [P < 0.001], anemia [P = 0.007], and delirium [P < 0.001]). When controlling for patient characteristics, TTS and mortality were similar between AI/AN and White patients (P = 0.31, P = 0.38, respectively). However, AI/AN patients had significantly more postoperative complications including stroke (P = 0.04) and pneumonia (P < 0.01), had a shorter length of stay (LOS) (P < 0.001), and were less likely to be discharged to a facility (P < 0.001). AI/AN patients with hip fractures had a higher burden of preoperative comorbidities and postoperative complications when compared with White patients. Reassuringly, AI/AN and White patients had similar TTS and 30-day mortality. When controlling for patient characteristics, AI/AN patients had a shorter LOS and were more likely to be discharged home. This may be inferred as a lack of access to rehabilitation facilities on discharge or more support from patient families and communities at home. Overall, AI/AN patients should be included in current and future research to better assess disparities in orthopaedic care.

cards.title: LIMBER: A Hybrid RNA Foundation Model for Predicting and Understanding RNA Structure and Function
cards.abstract: RNA foundation models offer a promising route to decoding the relationships between RNA sequence, structure and function, yet how model shapes the acquisition and organization of biological information remains poorly understood. Here we introduce Layer-Interleaved Mamba-Bidirectional Encoder for RNA (LIMBER), a hybrid foundation model integrating bidirectional self-attention with selective state-space modeling, pretrained on 40.5 million non-coding RNA sequences. Through task-specific fine-tuning, LIMBER achieves leading performance on secondary-structure prediction and non-coding RNA classification benchmarks, while demonstrating strong transferability to translation-related tasks and RNA--small-molecule interaction prediction. Beyond model development, we establish a unified, task-agnostic framework to systematically evaluate and interpret the biological knowledge intrinsically acquired by RNA foundation models. This framework validates LIMBER's strong capabilities in recovering RNA structures and predicting mutational effects, while uncovering a hierarchical, task-dependent organization of different biological information across model layers. By further systematically training and evaluating a broad panel of model variants spanning model capacity, training duration and dataset size, we uncover distinct scaling behaviors across structural, evolutionary and functional capabilities. Together, these findings establish LIMBER as a versatile RNA foundation model and provide broader insights into how architectural design, internal representations and scaling shape the learning of RNA sequence-structure-function relationships.

cards.title: MCseg: AI agent-guided workflow search for no-code cell segmentation and transcript attribution in spatial transcriptomics
cards.abstract: Cell-level analysis of high-resolution spatial transcriptomics depends on accurate segmentation and transcript assignment, yet current workflows often trade transcript capture for boundary purity and can require substantial image-analysis expertise. We developed MCseg, a downloadable no-code platform whose fixed segmentation engine was derived by an AI-agent-guided search in which an AI agent iteratively proposed and evaluated combinations of image-processing and segmentation operations against Xenium-derived cell boundaries. In a lung adenocarcinoma development set, fixed-parameter MCseg increased mean panoptic quality from 0.432 to 0.472 relative to an Optuna-tuned two-diameter Cellpose baseline, while a reference-guided calibration analysis reached 0.554. In an independent expert-annotated colorectal cancer region, MCseg showed higher lineage recall and micro-F1 than the StarDist-based ENACT workflow among cells covered by both methods. Across 15 colorectal cancer regions, MCseg increased neighborhood expression discordance and reduced lineage-exclusive co-expression relative to Space Ranger at similar UMI density. The fixed workflow also transferred to fresh-frozen breast cancer without tissue-specific architecture search, illustrating an agent-guided route to reproducible, locally deployable cell-level spatial transcriptomic analysis.

cards.title: Associations of Coexisting Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease and Sarcopenia-Related Abnormalities With Adverse Clinical Outcomes Across Obesity States.
cards.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is associated with adverse liver and non-liver outcomes, but the impact of coexisting sarcopenia-related abnormalities (e.g., low muscle strength [MS], muscle mass, and physical performance) remains unclear. In a prospective UK Biobank cohort (n = 438,748), we evaluated their joint associations with incidence and risks of all-cause mortality, cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), cardiovascular disease (CVD), chronic kidney disease (CKD), non-liver cancers, and obesity-related cancers across MASLD and sarcopenia-related abnormality status. Over a median follow-up of 13.8 years, 401 HCC, 1714 cirrhosis, 39,534 CVD, 19,637 CKD, 38,240 non-liver cancers, 12,536 obesity-related cancers, and 34,801 deaths occurred. A stepwise increase in both incidence and adjusted risk of liver and non-liver outcomes was observed across MASLD and sarcopenia strata. Within the coexistence group, the obesity (vs. non-obesity) subgroup generally had higher risks. For example, for cirrhosis, adjusted hazard ratios increased from 3.93 to 7.36 then 8.48 with MASLD alone, coexisting MASLD with low MS overall and coexisting MASLD, low MS and obesity, respectively. Similar findings were observed in external validation analyses using the 2011-2018 US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey cohort. Together, these observations inform risk stratification strategy and management of MASLD to include sarcopenia assessment.

cards.title: Neutrophil fate in bone infection: Mechanisms, microenvironment, and therapeutic opportunities.
cards.abstract: The clinical challenge of eradicating bone infection stems from microbial persistence within a distinct skeletal niche that is poorly perfused, hypoxic, mineralised, and highly susceptible to collateral damage. Neutrophils are central arbiters of this process and function as a double-edged sword: they are indispensable for initial pathogen containment, yet can become major drivers of chronic osteolysis, biofilm persistence, and inflammation when their effector programmes turn maladaptive. Recent high-resolution single-cell and spatial analyses have overturned the traditional view of neutrophils as short-lived, homogeneous cells, instead revealing a complex spectrum of functional states shaped by the infected bone microenvironment. In this Review, we use a neutrophil fate framework that distinguishes three related but non-equivalent levels: irreversible terminal fates, non-terminal tissue-disposition states and outcomes, and upstream fate-biasing states or processes. Terminal fates include apoptosis with subsequent efferocytic clearance, suicidal NETosis, pyroptosis, necroptosis, ferroptosis, mitochondrial permeability transition-driven necrosis, and secondary necrosis. By contrast, non-lytic (vital) NET release is considered an effector process rather than a terminal fate. Reverse migration is treated as a non-terminal tissue-exit outcome, whereas inflammatory retention is considered a non-terminal persistence state. Upstream fate-biasing factors include phenotypic or activation states, such as cellular ageing, NET-prone activation, and apoptosis delay, as well as regulatory processes including autophagy and metabolic or redox stress; none of these is classified as an independent terminal fate. We further examine how these terminal fates, non-terminal tissue-disposition states and outcomes, and upstream fate-biasing states and processes are spatially organised across osteomyelitic lesions and biofilm-associated interfaces, and how they govern interactions with osteoblasts, osteoclasts, and macrophages to determine the balance between antimicrobial control and progressive skeletal destruction. We also discuss emerging therapeutic paradigms aimed not at broadly suppressing neutrophil recruitment, but at precisely redirecting neutrophil fate, thereby providing a conceptual basis for stage-specific immunomodulation in orthopaedic infection. The Translational Potential of this Article This Review provides a fate-based framework for understanding how neutrophils shape the balance between pathogen control, biofilm persistence, osteolysis, and tissue repair in orthopaedic infection. By linking neutrophil fate programmes to distinct lesion microenvironments, including osteomyelitic lesions, implant-associated biofilms, contiguous soft-tissue infection, and fracture-related infection, this article highlights potential translational opportunities for stage- and compartment-specific immune modulation. These include improving patient stratification, guiding the timing of surgical source control and implant retention or removal, optimising dead-space management and local antimicrobial delivery, supporting vascularised soft-tissue reconstruction, and developing biomarkers that distinguish protective antimicrobial neutrophil responses from destructive inflammatory persistence. This framework may help shift future orthopaedic infection management from nonspecific suppression of inflammation toward precision redirection of maladaptive neutrophil fate while preserving early host defence and tissue repair capacity.

cards.title: Neferine Exerts a Protective Effect on Rat Osteoarthritis by Upregulating Autophagy.
cards.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a prevalent chronic joints disorder, characterized by progressive degeneration of articular cartilage accompanied by joint inflammation. The development of a safe and effective pharmacological therapy is highly anticipated. This research was designed to comprehensively investigate the function of NEF in regulating chondrocyte autophagy, along with its influence on the advancement of OA. In this study, a destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) surgery-induced osteoarthritis (OA) rat model and a tert-butyl hydroperoxide (TBHP)-stimulated primary rat chondrocyte model were established. By integrating network pharmacology, gene knockout, flow cytometry, and Western blotting analyses, the protective effects of neferine (NEF) against OA and its possible underlying molecular mechanisms were investigated. NEF effectively mitigates TBHP-induced chondrocyte apoptosis and senescence phenotypes while activating autophagy. Molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and gene knockdown experiments collectively suggest that NEF may enhance autophagy fluxes by inhibiting the downstream mTOR signaling pathway, thereby exerting partial protective effects against osteoarthritis. Furthermore, in a rat osteoarthritis model established through medial meniscus destabilization, NEF treatment greatly reduced the degeneration of articular cartilage caused by surgery. Collectively, these results indicate that NEF may enhance autophagy fluxes by inhibiting the mTOR signaling pathway, thereby exerting partial ameliorative effects on OA progression and highlighting its therapeutic potential for OA intervention.

cards.title: Intravital single-molecule microscopy reveals protein kinetics in live mammalian tissues
cards.abstract: Quantifying individual protein behavior in living mammalian tissues remains challenging. Here we introduce intravital single-molecule microscopy (iSiMM), an imaging and analysis framework that combines instant structured illumination microscopy guided tissue navigation with highly inclined and laminated optical sheet illumination. In live mice, iSiMM enables single-emitter detection and tracking of endogenously expressed fluorescently tagged proteins at 30 ms per frame. Trajectory-based modeling quantifies diffusion coefficients and model-defined bound and free fractions, while localization-density reconstructions map molecular organization. We illustrate the approach using the actomyosin cytoskeleton, resolving isoform-specific mobility and responses to physiological stimulation and genetic perturbation. Single-molecule detection in pancreas and skeletal muscle, including after in vivo transfection, further demonstrates feasibility across additional tissues and labeling strategies. iSiMM provides a framework for investigating molecular behavior in the physiological context of living mammalian tissues.

cards.title: A pilot study of a computed tomography volumetric analysis technique to determine severity of injury and prognosis for OTA 42A-C open tibial diaphyseal fractures.
cards.abstract: This pilot study evaluated a novel computed tomography (CT)-based volumetric analysis tool for open tibial fractures. We hypothesized that the volumetric injury ratio (VINJ/VUNINJ), a quantitative comparison of injured with contralateral uninjured limb segments, would correlate with clinical outcomes and serve as a prognostic marker. A retrospective review of a tibial fracture registry was conducted at a single academic institution (2014-2024). Eligible patients were older than 18 years old with preoperative bilateral lower extremity CT imaging, high-energy injuries, and ≥6 months of follow-up. Demographics, Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), injury features, and outcomes including fracture-related infection (FRI), amputation, and nonunion were collected. Tissue volume was measured at the fracture midpoint and 5 cm proximal and distal, with corresponding contralateral measurements. VINJ/VUNINJ was calculated, and logistic regression estimated complication risk. The primary endpoint was a composite complication (FRI, amputation, or nonunion). Discrimination was assessed using AUROC and compared with the Gustilo-Anderson (GA) classification via the DeLong test. The Youden Index identified an optimal risk threshold. Power analysis estimated sample size requirements for a future validation study. Fifteen patients met inclusion criteria (mean age 36.1 ± 13.5 years). GA distribution: 60% II, 6.7% IIIa, 26.7% IIIb, and 6.7% IIIc. The volumetric model (log[p/(1-p)] = -110.964 + 100.011 × VINJ/VUNINJ) demonstrated a trend toward improved discriminatory ability compared with the GA model (AUROC: 0.944 vs 0.769, P = 0.068). A Youden-derived threshold (0.539) classified 5 patients (33.3%) as high-risk; all developed complications compared with 10% in the low-risk group (100% vs 10%, P = 0.001). Power analysis indicated that detecting a twofold increase in complications would require ∼23 patients per arm (46 total). This pilot study introduces a CT-based volumetric ratio as a quantitative tool for risk stratification in open tibial fractures. Findings suggest superior prognostic accuracy compared with GA, supporting prospective validation in larger patient cohorts.

cards.title: Association between surgery-oriented standardized clinical pathways and postoperative delirium in geriatric hip fracture patients: A retrospective cohort study.
cards.abstract: Elderly hip fracture patients are at high risk of postoperative delirium (POD). The association between surgery-oriented standardized clinical pathways and POD incidence remains poorly clarified. This study aimed to explore the association between surgery-oriented standardized clinical pathways, internal fixation clinical pathway(IFCP), versus arthroplasty clinical pathway(ARCP), and POD occurrence in elderly hip fracture patients. This retrospective cohort study examined the medical records of patients aged 65 years and older who underwent hip fracture surgery at a tertiary medical facility from January 2022 to December 2025. Patients were divided into groups according to the surgery-oriented standardized clinical pathways they received: those with extracapsular fractures who underwent intramedullary nailing were assigned to the IFCP group, and those with intracapsular fractures who underwent hip arthroplasty were assigned to the ARCP group. Multivariate logistic regression and propensity score matching (PSM) analyses were utilized to evaluate the association between surgery-oriented standardized clinical pathways and POD. Subgroup analysis was subsequently conducted to explore potential interactions further. A total of 693 patients were included in this study, with a POD incidence of 15.01% (104/693) during the postoperative hospitalization period. Before matching, the incidence of POD was significantly lower in the ARCP group than in the IFCP group (9.92% vs. 20.61%, P < 0.001). This significant difference persisted after matching (11.54% vs. 18.85%, P = 0.020). Multivariate logistic regression confirmed that the ARCP was independently associated with a reduced risk of POD (OR = 0.40, 95% CI: 0.24-0.67, P < 0.001). Surgery-oriented standardized clinical pathways showed a statistically association with POD risk among elderly hip fracture patients. The ARCP exhibited a lower observed incidence of POD compared with the IFCP.

cards.title: Route of Chronic Corticosteroid Administration and Risk of Hip Avascular Necrosis: A National Comparison of Oral Versus Intravenous Exposure.
cards.abstract: Avascular necrosis (AVN) results from compromised blood supply to bone and may progress to arthritis requiring arthroplasty. Although chronic steroid exposure is a well-established risk factor of AVN, the relative risk of administration route remains poorly understood. This study characterizes the 10-year incidence of hip AVN and subsequent total hip arthroplasty (THA) following chronic oral versus intravenous (IV) steroid exposure. Adult patients with ≥10 years of continuous follow-up in a national claims database were stratified into oral, IV, or steroid-naive cohorts. Chronic oral exposure was defined as ≥5 mg daily for ≥90 days; chronic IV exposure as ≥90 days of high-dose therapy delivered in multiple 3- to 5-day courses with no inter-course gap >30 days. Controls were randomly sampled from eligible individuals without chronic corticosteroid exposure. Patients with prior AVN or femoral neck fractures were excluded. Kaplan-Meier analysis estimated 10-year hip AVN incidence. Multivariable Cox models evaluated hip AVN risk by comparing steroid exposure adjusting for age, sex, Elixhauser Comorbidity Index (ECI), and established AVN risk factors. Among patients who developed AVN, oral and IV steroid users were exact matched on age, sex, ECI, and AVN risk factors. Kaplan-Meier analysis estimated 10-year incidence of THA after AVN diagnosis. Among 2,377,126 patients, 1,745,312 were steroid naive, 15,570 received IV steroids, and 616,244 received oral steroids. Ten-year AVN incidence was 0.43% in controls, 0.75% in IV steroid users, and 1.02% in oral steroid users. After adjustment, both IV (HR 1.73; 95% CI 1.44-2.09; p < 0.001) and oral (HR 2.25; 95% CI 2.17-2.34; p < 0.001) chronic steroid exposure remained independently associated with increased hip AVN risk. Ten-year THA incidence following AVN did not differ significantly between IV and oral steroid users (27.7% vs. 18.6%; p = 0.40). Both chronic IV and oral steroid use were associated with elevated 10-year risk of hip AVN, with the greatest risk following oral exposure. These findings support minimizing cumulative steroid exposure and surveillance in patients receiving long-term steroids. Level IV. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

cards.title: Mosaicplasty of the Femoral Head Via the Direct Anterior Approach.
cards.abstract: Mosaicplasty of the femoral head is a cartilage restoration procedure for focal osteochondral lesions, particularly in young, active patients. Although commonly performed in the knee, its use in the hip is rare because of technical difficulty and limited exposure. Historically, access required invasive surgical dislocation with a trochanteric osteotomy, as described by Ganz et al.6,7; however, the direct anterior approach (DAA) offers a minimally invasive, muscle-sparing alternative2,8. In the example in the present video article, we describe the use of an original technique for the treatment of a 1-cm2 posttraumatic osteochondral lesion in the weight-bearing dome of the left femoral head. A mosaicplasty procedure was performed via the DAA. The patient was positioned supine on a fracture table for precise leg manipulation. A 7-cm incision was made anterolaterally. After capsular exposure, the lesion site was debrided, and a cylindrical recipient socket was drilled perpendicularly to a depth of 12 mm. An autograft plug was harvested from the anteroinferior femoral head and inserted with use of a plunger. An additional allograft plug was utilized to complete the defect filling at the donor site. Capsular and soft-tissue closure was performed in layers. Surgical alternatives include microfracture, which promotes fibrocartilage regeneration11; autologous chondrocyte implantation1; fresh osteochondral allograft transplantation10; and total hip arthroplasty, particularly in advanced-stage cases. Nonoperative alternatives include physiotherapy, the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, activity modification, and intra-articular injections. Compared with other procedures, mosaicplasty restores native hyaline cartilage, providing superior biomechanical properties and potentially more durable outcomes3. The DAA avoids the need for an extensive approach and surgical dislocation and, as such, reduces risks such as osteonecrosis5. Additionally, harvesting grafts from the ipsilateral femoral head may reduce donor-site morbidity compared with harvesting from the knee9. This approach is well suited for small, isolated lesions in younger patients in whom joint preservation is preferred2,4,8. Patients can expect pain reduction, restoration of function, and return to normal activities. In the present example, the patient achieved pain-free ambulation by 3 months postoperatively, with no limp and stable grafts on radiographs. Similar outcomes have been reported in small case series, showing good to excellent early results3,5,8. However, long-term durability remains to be determined. Use a traction table for leg control and access optimization.Preserve the ascending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery to reduce the risk of osteonecrosis.Ensure perpendicular drilling of the recipient site for graft stability.Avoid mosaicplasty for lesions of >2 cm2, as mosaicplasty in these lesions has shown diminished clinical improvement8. THA = total hip arthroplastyAVN = osteonecrosisACI = autologous chondrocyte implantationCT = computed tomographyMRI = magnetic resonance imagingASIS = anterior superior iliac spine.

cards.title: Hybrid multimodal exercise training promotes enhanced recovery after surgery and improves musculoskeletal strength in patients with osteosarcopenic obesity: A clinical study protocol.
cards.abstract: Osteosarcopenic obesity (OSO) is a progressive, systemic condition characterized by declines in skeletal muscle mass, strength, and function, accompanied by bone loss and adipose tissue accumulation, leading to adverse health outcomes including frailty, poor quality of life, high fracture risk, poor postoperative recovery, and mortality. It is more common in older adults, with physical inactivity and malnutrition being the main etiological factors, especially lack of exercise. Regular physical activity combined with appropriate dietary intervention is necessary to achieve optimal therapeutic effects for OSO. However, conventional exercise may be difficult for older adults with OSO who often present with frailty, and little is known about the role of exercise in promoting enhanced recovery after surgery and improving musculoskeletal strength in OSO patients. Hybrid multimodal exercise training, which involves targeted training based on an individual's physical and health status, may benefit bone, muscle, and quality of life. This clinical study investigates the feasibility and effectiveness of hybrid multimodal exercise training in promoting enhanced recovery after surgery and improving musculoskeletal strength in patients with osteosarcopenic obesity. One hundred and twenty older adults diagnosed with OSO will be assigned to two groups: a hybrid multimodal exercise training group and a usual care group. Assessments will be conducted in the hospital, including baseline and post-intervention evaluations of health and function (body composition, bone mineral density, frailty score, balance ability, short physical performance battery, timed up-and-go test, activities of daily living). OSO patients will undergo a combined exercise intervention primarily based on resistance training in hospital and community settings for 12 months. Most older adults lack regular physical activity, leading to progressive muscle atrophy, impaired physical function, and substantially limited daily mobility. This initiates a vicious cycle wherein frailty, poor physical performance, sarcopenia, osteoporosis and adiposity reinforce each other, rendering structured exercise training extremely difficult for older adults. Unlike conventional combined training regimens that simply stack independent exercise modalities, this study implemented a hybrid multimodal exercise intervention. Hybrid multimodal exercise training (HMET) is a 12-month, supervised, progressive structured exercise intervention that systematically integrates resistance training, aerobic training, balance training, and flexibility training. It is designed to improve musculoskeletal strength, bone mineral density, body composition, and functional outcomes following enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) in patients with osteosarcopenic obesity (OSO). The four components are allocated within each training session according to a prespecified ratio, with periodic progression of training load to sustain adaptive responses.Characterized by low entry barriers, the intervention is easy for older adults to start, well-suited to daily life, and requires little specialized equipment. Patient functional status will be assessed using the Fatigue, Resistance, Ambulation, Illness and Loss of Weight Index (FRAIL), Tinetti Performance Oriented Mobility Assessment (POMA), Timed Up and Go Test (TUG), Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB), and Activities of Daily Living (ADL) scale. Body composition will be measured by multi-frequency bioelectrical impedance analysis. Bone quality will be assessed by measuring vertebral HU values using energy CT, and bone mineral density T-scores of the lumbar spine and femoral neck will be analyzed by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA). Our study protocol has been registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR), a primary registry of the WHO International Clinical Trial Registry Platform (ICTRP). Registration website: https://www.chictr.org.cn/. Registration number: ChiCTR2600116975. The study protocol and statistical analysis plan (SAP) are available on this website.
