cards.title: <scp>YBX1</scp> ‐Enriched <scp>iPSC</scp> ‐Derived Exosomes Rejuvenate Senescent Airway Basal Stem Cells in Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis
cards.abstract: ABSTRACT Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is characterized by pronounced senescence of airway tissue stem cells, thereby accelerating disease progression and impairing endogenous repair. Although previous studies have shown that exosomes derived from pluripotent stem cells can attenuate adult tissue stem cell senescence in animal models, direct assessments of their impact on senescence and stemness in human IPF patient‐derived tissue stem cells under pathophysiologically relevant conditions remain lacking. In this study, we used adult airway tissue stem cells (KRT5 + basal stem cells) isolated from IPF patients as the primary model to systematically study the functional activities of iPSC‐derived exosomes (iPSC‐Exos) and MSC‐derived exosomes (MSC‐Exos). We found that iPSC‐Exos robustly reversed the senescent phenotype and restored stemness in patient‐derived KRT5 + basal cells in 2D and 3D (precision‐cut lung slices) IPF physiological models, whereas MSC‐Exos showed minimal effects. Mechanistic analyses revealed several phenomena: YBX1 was enriched in iPSC‐Exos, both YBX1 and NFYB increased in iPSC‐Exo‐treated basal cells, YBX1 overexpression in basal cells recapitulated part of the anti‐senescence phenotype, and interference with NF‐Y DNA binding partially attenuated the response. This study provides an ideal paradigm for elucidating how exosomes from high‐stemness stem cells restore low‐stemness cell function and presents a clinically translatable strategy for tissue regeneration in age‐related pathologies.

cards.title: <scp>KLRG1</scp> and Helios Together With <scp>CD45RA</scp> and <scp>CD28</scp> Nuance Classification of <scp>CD8</scp> <sup>+</sup> T‐Cell Populations, Revealing Age‐ and <scp>CMV</scp> ‐Driven Functional Remodeling
cards.abstract: ABSTRACT Immunosenescence severely compromises immune protection in older adults and is hallmarked by extensive remodeling of the CD8 + T‐cell compartment. This is characterized by a decline in naïve cells and an expansion of Temra cells, which associates with a shift from TCR toward bystander responsiveness. Traditionally, the T‐cell differentiation state has been defined by expression of CD45RA and CD27, sometimes supplemented by CD28. However, this conventional classification may not fully capture the functional heterogeneity and age‐related changes among CD8 + T cells. Additional aging‐related markers, such as TIGIT, Helios, KIR, KLRG1, CD56, and NKG2A, may provide a more accurate picture of T‐cell remodeling. Here, we performed comprehensive phenotypic and functional profiling of human CD8 + T cells and demonstrate that KLRG1 and Helios, in combination with CD28 and CD45RA, allows for a more detailed classification of CD8 + T‐cell populations. These markers delineate nine functionally distinct CD8 + T‐cell populations with unique responsiveness to TCR‐ and cytokine‐mediated stimulation. The frequencies of these populations are differentially shaped by age and CMV serostatus, resulting in a shift from broad and strong responses toward weaker, more restricted, and predominantly cytotoxic responses, in older or CMV‐positive individuals. Importantly, in a cohort of adults aged 60+, these compositional changes are associated with a decreased likelihood of mounting effective T‐cell responses following influenza vaccination. Our findings provide new insights into CD8 + T‐cell remodeling following aging and CMV infection and highlight the value of adding KLRG1 and Helios as markers for improved immunomonitoring and potential intervention targets later in life.

cards.title: A pragmatic resistance band intervention to improve physical function in community-dwelling older adults: A randomized controlled trial.
cards.abstract: Resistance training can slow sarcopenic decline and is a foundational lifestyle habit for maintaining health span and independence, yet participation remains low. We examined the effectiveness of an 18-week faded-contact resistance-band training program on physical function in community-dwelling preclinically mobility-limited older adults. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) was conducted in older adults with self-reported preclinical mobility limitation (≥70 years), comparing a resistance band training (RBT) group with a non-exercise control (CON) group. The RBT group participated in a twice-weekly, 18-week, faded-contact, group-based full-body resistance band program. The primary outcome was physical function. Secondary outcomes included strength, power, body composition, sarcopenia risk, frailty status, mobility, habitual physical activity, and health-related quality of life, assessed at Week 0, 6, 12, and 18. Sixty participants were randomized, and 59 (mean age 75 ± 4 years; 66% women) were analyzed (RBT n = 30; CON n = 29). Adherence to RBT was 91%. RBT improved function from week 0-12 in the Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) (0.88 [95% CI: 0.29, 1.47]; p = 0.001) and tandem stand (0.62 [95% CI: 0.17, 1.07]; p = 0.003). The RBT group significantly improved in the 5 times sit-to-stand compared to CON from week 0-6 (-2.01 [95% CI: -3.34, -0.67]; p = 0.001), week 12 (-2.61 [95% CI: -3.95, -1.27]; p < 0.001), and week 18 (-1.85 [95% CI: -3.19, -0.50]; p = 0.003). At 18 weeks, D3-Creatine-measured muscle mass increased more in RBT than CON (1.07 kg [95% CI: 0.49, 1.65]; p < 0.001). RBT also improved relative sit-to-stand power compared to CON at weeks 6, 12, and 18, with the largest difference at week 12 (0.55 W/kg [95% CI: 0.28, 0.83]; p < 0.001). No interactions were observed for other secondary outcomes. Clinically relevant SPPB change occurred only in RBT. A pragmatic resistance-band training program delivered by exercise and health professionals to preclinically mobility-limited older adults increased physical function and D3-Creatine-measured muscle mass. These data provide insight into the effectiveness of resistance band training for maintaining and improving function and muscle mass.

cards.title: Leucine-enriched whey protein, creatine, and exercise in sarcopenia: an integrative view of the aging muscle–immune–brain axis
cards.abstract: Aging is accompanied by progressive alterations in skeletal muscle mass, neuromuscular function, metabolic homeostasis, and immune regulation, contributing to the development of sarcopenia and functional decline. Exercise represents a key strategy for preserving muscle health; however, nutritional factors may modify exercise-induced adaptations, particularly in the context of age-related anabolic resistance and altered immunometabolic signaling. This review examines emerging evidence on the potential interactions of leucine-enriched whey protein and creatine monohydrate with exercise within the aging muscle–immune–brain axis. Particular emphasis is placed on immunometabolic remodeling, inflammaging, myokine–immune crosstalk, and molecular pathways involved in muscle adaptation, including mammalian target of rapamycin-related protein synthesis and cellular energy metabolism. The review also considers how these nutritional strategies, in conjunction with exercise, may influence mitochondrial function, oxidative stress, inflammatory signaling, and muscle-derived communication with the brain. Emerging evidence further suggests possible links between exercise, nutritional modulation, myokine signaling, and processes relevant to cognitive and neuromuscular function. By integrating these interconnected pathways, this review highlights current mechanistic perspectives on how exercise and targeted nutritional strategies may contribute to the maintenance of neuromuscular resilience during aging and in sarcopenia. Because direct human evidence that leucine-enriched whey protein or creatine modulates myokine, extracellular vesicle, gut microbial, or cognitive pathways is limited, the integrated muscle–immune–brain model is presented as a hypothesis-generating framework rather than as an established mechanism.

cards.title: Diagnostic performance of liver virtual non-contrast and virtual unenhanced reconstructions derived from photon-counting detector CT of the upper abdomen.
cards.abstract: Photon-counting detector computed tomography (PCD-CT) enables native spectral imaging with the generation of virtual non-contrast (VNC) images from contrast-enhanced acquisitions. Two reconstruction algorithms are currently available, Virtual Unenhanced (VUE) and Liver Virtual Non-Contrast (LVNC), but their reliability compared with True Non-Contrast (TNC) imaging in abdominal applications remains incompletely established. This study evaluated the quantitative accuracy, image quality, and potential clinical impact of VNC reconstructions derived from PCD-CT. In this retrospective single-center study, 150 patients, of whom 140 were included for the analyses, underwent multiphasic PCD-CT including TNC, arterial, and portal venous phases. VNC datasets were generated from arterial and venous acquisitions using the VUE and LVNC algorithms. Tissue attenuation, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) were compared with TNC images. The agreement of VNC reconstructions with TNC-based classification criteria for hepatic steatosis, myosteatosis, and osteoporosis was also evaluated. Significant attenuation differences were observed between TNC and VNC reconstructions across most tissues. The smallest errors were found in soft tissues, particularly the liver and spleen, whereas the largest discrepancies occurred in vascular and osseous structures. SNR was higher on VNC than on TNC images in the liver, spleen and paravertebral muscle but lower in several other tissues, whereas CNR was higher with LVNCa and lower with VUEv than with TNC. VUE most closely reproduced TNC attenuation in the liver and spleen, whereas LVNC systematically underestimated attenuation in iodine-enhancing organs. Agreement with TNC-based criteria for hepatic steatosis, myosteatosis and osteoporosis required reconstruction-specific cut-offs, which should be considered exploratory. Omitting TNC could potentially reduce radiation exposure by 16.5% for upper abdomen and 21.2% for total abdominal examinations. VUE reconstructions showed good agreement with TNC attenuation in the liver and spleen in both contrast phases, whereas LVNC systematically underestimated attenuation in iodine-enhancing organs and was closer to TNC than VUE only in subcutaneous fat and venous-phase muscle. Substantial bias in vascular and bone structures limits the interchangeability of both algorithms with TNC imaging. VNC may support a potential reduction in radiation dose when replacing a planned TNC acquisition; since lesion detection and characterization were not evaluated, the safe omission of TNC was not demonstrated.

cards.title: Socioeconomic inequality in osteoporosis among Iranian older adults: Bushehr Elderly Health (BEH) Program.
cards.abstract: Socioeconomic status (SES) may affect bone density, but evidence in older Iranians is limited. This study of 2,266 Bushehr Elderly Health cohort participants found marked inequalities in osteoporosis and low bone mineral density (BMD), disproportionately concentrated among participants with lower socioeconomic status. SES gap was largely driven by age and sex. Findings emphasize the need for equity-oriented screening and social policies. SES is associated with many chronic conditions, yet its role in bone health among older Iranians is poorly characterized. This study quantifies SES-related inequalities in BMD using BEH program data. In this cross-sectional analysis of 2266 BEH program participants, BMD was measured by DXA at lumbar spine, femoral neck, and total hip. Osteoporosis was defined as T-score ≤ -2.5 and low BMD as T-score ≤ -1.0. SES was estimated using a PCA-derived SES index quintile. Inequality was assessed with concentration indices and Lorenz curves. Multivariable logistic regression, adjusted for DAG-identified confounders, examined SES-osteoporosis associations. Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition quantified covariate contributions to gaps between lowest and highest SES quintiles. Participants' mean age was 69.3 ± 6.3 years, and 51.9% were female. The prevalence of osteoporosis and low BMD were 30.9% and 74.1%, respectively. Negative concentration indices indicated that osteoporosis (CI = -0.11, p < 0.001) and low BMD (CI = -0.048, p < 0.001) were disproportionately concentrated among participants with lower socioeconomic status. Adjusted odds ratios (highest vs. lowest SES quintile) were 0.96 (p = 0.815) for osteoporosis and 0.67 (p = 0.037) for low BMD. SES gaps of 10.4% (osteoporosis) and 10.7% (low BMD) were largely explained by sex and age. Marked socioeconomic inequalities in bone health, disproportionately affecting older adults with lower socioeconomic status, were observed in southern Iran. Demographic factors account for much of the disparity, underscoring the need for equitable screening, education, and social interventions.

cards.title: Access to positron emission tomography combined with computed tomography in the management of lung cancer in Te Manawa Taki Midland Region of New Zealand.
cards.abstract: This study examines access to 18-F fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography-computed tomography (FDG PET-CT; PET-CT) scans among lung cancer patients. Patients diagnosed with lung cancer in 2011-2021 were identified from the Midland Lung Cancer Register and the New Zealand Cancer Registry. Patients were linked to the National Non-Admitted Patient Collection to determine if they underwent PET-CT. Logistic regression was used to estimate the odds ratios of having PET-CT, adjusting for age, gender, ethnicity, year of diagnosis, socio-economic status, cancer stage, cell type, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) status and comorbidities. We identified 613 patients with stage I, 300 with stage II and 3,722 with stages III and IV lung cancer, with 75% of stage I and 68.3% of stage II undergoing PET-CT. PET-CT has become more common over time. Patients aged 80 years and over, Māori, those with frailty (ECOG 2+), and those with stages II-IV of disease were less likely to receive PET-CT. Gender, socio-economic status and comorbidities did not influence the use of PET-CT. PET-CT is a standard of care for patients with early-stage lung cancer, suitable for curative treatment. The disparity of access to PET-CT for Māori needs to be addressed.

cards.title: PP2A-dependent downregulation of GABAB receptors modulates somatostatin interneurons function and plasticity.
cards.abstract: Cortical circuits require precise inhibitory and excitatory neurotransmission to encode information and prevent pathology. Metabotropic GABAB receptors (GABABRs) are key inhibitory regulators in mammalian neurons. In GABAergic interneurons (INs), GABABR activation reduces inhibition, leading to disinhibitory mechanisms. Hippocampal somatostatin-expressing (SST) INs provide feedback inhibition to distal dendrites of principal cells (PCs) and other INs. Plasticity of SST INs is well established to control hippocampal circuit function dependent on metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs) and GABABRs. Whether GABABRs regulate SST INs function over longer time scales and if this influences circuit function remains unclear. We combine quantitative freeze-fracture replica immunoelectron microscopy, ex vivo electrophysiology, and pharmacology to show that GABABR activation regulates long-term potentiation (LTP) of SST INs through protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A)-dependent loss of cell-surface GABABR, mGluR1α receptors, and Cav1.2 (L-type) Ca2+ channels. GABABR loss in SST INs shifts hippocampal activity toward greater plasticity of long-range inputs to CA1.

cards.title: Aging drives distinct chromatin signatures of CD8 T cell dysfunction and the emergence of a unique CD8 T <sub>reg</sub> cell population
cards.abstract: Aging profoundly alters CD8 T cells, driving senescence and exhaustion that contribute to immune decline. By mapping chromatin accessibility across functional and dysfunctional CD8 T cell subsets from young and aged mice, we found that age-related CD8 T cell dysfunction was associated with a loss of regulation at three distinct levels. Dysfunctional CD8 T cells showed reduced accessibility of genes essential for “stemness,” indicating diminished regenerative potential. Exhausted memory T cells (T mem cells) showed decreased accessibility of “restraint” genes, which limit differentiation postactivation. Last, both senescent virtual memory T cells (T VM cells) and exhausted T mem cells displayed increased accessibility of “terminal inhibitory” genes, underscoring progression toward irreversible dysfunction. The inhibitory receptor gene Fcgr2b , encoding FcγRIIb/CD32b, was notably increased in a subset of aged T VM cells with regulatory characteristics. This study defines mechanisms of CD8 T cell aging and identifies a CD8 regulatory T cell (T reg cell) population that emerges as a hallmark of aging.

cards.title: Sit-to-stand performance and gait symmetry in older adults with sarcopenia and sarcopenic obesity: A cross-sectional comparative study of lower limb motor function.
cards.abstract: Sarcopenic obesity (SO), characterized by the concurrent presence of diminished muscle mass and excessive adiposity, poses an increased risk to physical function, balance, and fall susceptibility in older adults. Although sarcopenia alone has been linked to mobility impairments, the specific effects of elevated body fat on sit-to-stand (STS) performance and gait symmetry have not been thoroughly investigated. This study sought to compare STS ability and gait symmetry between older adults with sarcopenia alone (SP group) and the SO group, and to analyze the biomechanical and neuromuscular differences associated with varying levels of body fat. A cohort of 60 elderly individuals diagnosed with sarcopenia was stratified into SP and SO groups according to the Chinese diagnostic criteria for sarcopenia and obesity. Functional performance was assessed using the Berg Balance Scale (BBS), the Five Times Sit-to-Stand Test, the Timed Up and Go Test, and phase-specific STS timing. Gait and plantar pressure symmetry indices were evaluated utilizing motion capture and pedobarographic systems. The SO group demonstrated significantly lower BBS scores, extended durations for the Five Times Sit-to-Stand Test and Timed Up and Go Test, and prolonged STS phase times (P < .05). Additionally, this group exhibited reduced knee joint angular velocities and increased asymmetry in the stance phase, swing phase, single-limb support, and foot rotation (P < .05). No significant differences were observed in the symmetry indices for step length and step time. Sarcopenic obesity was associated with poorer sit-to-stand performance and greater gait asymmetry in older adults compared with sarcopenia alone. Body composition assessment and gait analysis may provide complementary information for functional evaluation.

cards.title: Age is Just a Number: Treatment Considerations for Older Adults with Inflammatory Bowel Disease.
cards.abstract: The purpose of this review is to synthesize the recent evidence regarding efficacy and safety of advanced therapies and surgical interventions in older adults with IBD, as well as examine how geriatric factors (frailty, multimorbidity, polypharmacy, and patient priorities) should influence the selection of therapies in this population. Ongoing inflammation is often a key driver of adverse outcomes in older adults with IBD, and the efficacy of biologics and small molecules is generally preserved in this population. Treatment selection should therefore prioritize efficacy while also accounting for comorbidities, infection and malignancy risk, and potential drug interactions; chronological age alone should not limit their use. Early surgery may also benefit appropriately selected patients, while functional assessment can identify those suitable for immediate intervention and those who may benefit from preoperative optimization. Across treatment decisions, the geriatric 5Ms, multicomplexity, medications, mobility, mind, and what matters most, can help guide individualized care. Treatment of older adults with IBD is complex and multidimensional. Management paradigms should shift away from therapeutic hesitancy on the basis of chronological age alone and towards an individualized approach that prioritizes effective disease control and symptom relief, thereby preserving function, independence, and promoting healthy aging for older adults with IBD.

cards.title: Lumbar Anterior Column Reconstruction With Expandable Cage Placement and Cerclage Wire Augmentation: A Case Report.
cards.abstract: A 31-year-old man with a traumatic L5 burst fracture underwent initial posterior and anterior reconstruction, complicated by early anterior cage migration. This prompted revision with bilateral cerclage wires securing the cage to posterior rods. At 1-year follow-up, implants remained stable. Anterior column reconstruction at the lumbosacral junction is technically demanding, particularly in patients with high sacral slope, leading to increased shear forces and risk of cage migration. We present a novel technique using cerclage wire fixation to stabilize an expandable cage following L5 corpectomy. This offers a safe adjunct to enhance cage stability in complex lumbosacral reconstructions.

cards.title: Cell division timing shapes the morphology and size of nascent multicellular organisms
cards.abstract: Upon making the transition from unicellularity to multicellularity, many previously optimized cellular traits experience the renewed scrutiny of natural selection due to their novel effects on multicellular phenotypes. However, we lack a comprehensive understanding of how and why specific cellular traits influence multicellular phenotypes and fitness. The snowflake yeast model system provides a tractable entry point for such investigations because cluster size is governed by simple topological and mechanical constraints and the connections between some cell-level traits (cellular aspect ratio, cell volume, bud neck strength) and group-level traits (group size) have been well characterized. However, differences in these known properties are insufficient to explain the difference in cluster size between the two strains that serve as the ancestors of the ongoing Multicellularity Long-Term Evolution Experiment (MuLTEE). Using time-lapse microscopy and single cell tracking, we identify cell division timing as a cellular trait that strongly influences multicellular morphology and size in snowflake yeast. The "petite" snowflake yeast ancestor divides asynchronously, with a 28% longer first division, while the "grande" ancestor divides synchronously. Using network theoretical and biophysical models, we show that strains exhibiting a first division delay generate more highly-branched network topologies, accelerating the accumulation of crowding-induced mechanical stress, resulting in clusters that fracture at smaller sizes. Conversely, synchronously dividing strains produce more symmetric, larger clusters. Synchronous cell division can provide benefits through both faster growth and larger size, suggesting multiple potential selective pathways for its evolution. Furthermore, we explore how accelerated first division can produce even larger groups and how another unexpected mechanism for modifying cluster topology, apoptosis rate, can exert a similar effect. Our results identify cell division timing as a previously underappreciated axis of phenotypic variation that strongly influences multicellular morphology and reproduction in the snowflake yeast system. This suggests that temporal regulation of cell division may be an evolutionarily accessible mechanism for early control of morphogenesis in nascent multicellular organisms with permanent intercellular bonds.

cards.title: The overlap between frailty and dementia, and impact on hospitalisation and mortality
cards.abstract: Background: Dementia and frailty frequently coexist, and each increases hospitalisation and mortality risk. We examined frailty prevalence among people with dementia in England, and whether its associations with hospitalisation and mortality differ from those in people without dementia. Methods: Using Clinical Practice Research Datalink primary care data linked to hospital and mortality records, we matched people with dementia to controls by year of birth, sex, and practice, and measured frailty using the electronic Frailty Index. We modelled hospitalisation episodes and total bed days and mortality, and tested effect modification by ethnicity, deprivation, and rurality. Results: In 2021, 58.1% of people with dementia were living with frailty, compared with 29.4% in controls. In outcome analyses (556,685 people with dementia and 1,526,612 controls), among people with dementia, severe versus no frailty was associated with more hospitalisation episodes (aIRR 1.47, 95% CI 1.45,1.50) and higher mortality (aHR 1.58, 1.54,1.62). Mild and moderate frailty were associated with slightly fewer bed days (aIRR 0.96, 0.95,0.97; 0.99, 0.97,0.99) and severe frailty with more (aIRR 1.04, 1.01,1.07). Associations were stronger among controls (severe frailty: episodes aIRR 3.07, 2.99,3.14; bed days 3.28, 3.17,3.38; mortality aHR 2.74, 2.66,2.82). Conclusions: Frailty is common among people with dementia and associated with more hospital admissions and higher mortality. Its relationship with bed days is more complex, possibly reflecting difficulties discharging people with dementia home rather than to residential care. Frailty assessment and management should be a core part of dementia care.

cards.title: Development and Internal Validation of a Prediction Model for Reversible Cognitive Frailty in People Living with HIV.
cards.abstract: Reversible cognitive frailty may be an important target for early identification among people with HIV (PWH). We developed a prediction model for reversible cognitive frailty and assessed its internal validity using clinical, laboratory, and medication-related data. Positive Brain Health Now cohort, including adults recruited from five Canadian HIV clinics between 2013 and 2018. Data from 824 adults with HIV aged 35 years or older were analysed. Reversible cognitive frailty was defined as co-occurring physical frailty and self-reported cognitive difficulty without dementia. Twenty candidate predictors were entered into least absolute shrinkage and selection operator logistic regression (LASSO) with 10-fold cross-validation to select the final predictor set. Internal validity was assessed through discrimination (apparent and optimism-corrected C-statistic via bootstrap resampling), calibration, and clinical utility (decision curve analysis). Reversible cognitive frailty was present in 7.5% of participants. The final model retained 10 predictors; the strongest were female sex, greater comorbidity burden, higher anxiety and depression scores, and higher anticholinergic medication burden, with additional contributions from hepatic, nutritional, HIV-related, and medication variables. On internal assessment, the model showed strong discrimination (optimism-corrected C-statistic 0.882), acceptable calibration, and net benefit over assess-all and assess-none strategies. At the optimal threshold, sensitivity was 91.9%, specificity 76.1%, and negative predictive value 99.1%. This is the first prediction model developed for reversible cognitive frailty in PWH, showing strong discrimination, acceptable calibration, and clinical utility within the development cohort. External validation in independent samples is needed before clinical use.

cards.title: Association between genetic variant in estrogen receptor alpha gene and bone texture in bushehr elderly health (BEH) cohort.
cards.abstract: Osteoporosis is a multifactorial skeletal disorder influenced by genetic and environmental factors. The estrogen receptor alpha (α) encoded by the ESR1 gene is a key regulator of bone remodeling, and the association between its PvuII polymorphism (rs2234693 T > C) and osteoporosis remains controversial. This case-control study investigated the association between the ESR1 rs2234693 (PvuII) polymorphism and osteoporosis in 475 (138 osteoporotic and 337 non-osteoporotic) participants aged ≥ 50 years from the Bushehr Elderly Cohort, southern Iran. Genotype distributions did not differ significantly between osteoporotic and non-osteoporotic participants. No significant association was observed between ESR1 rs2234693 and osteoporosis. However, individuals carrying the TT genotype exhibited a higher prevalence of normal Trabecular Bone Score (TBS) (61.8%) compared with carriers of the TC (47.3%) and CC (47.2%) genotypes. Conversely, the frequency of C allele was significantly more frequent among individuals with reduced TBS, TT (38.2%), TC (52.7%) and CC (52.85%). Significant differences in allele and genotype frequencies remained evident after adjusting for age, body mass index (BMI), sex, and serum vitamin D levels. The ESR1 rs2234693 (PvuII) polymorphism was not associated with bone mineral density (BMD)-defined osteoporosis but was significantly associated with reduced TBS, suggesting that its effects may be more pronounced on trabecular bone microarchitecture than on BMD. These findings support the complementary role of TBS in evaluating the skeletal effects of ESR1 genetic variation. Further large-scale studies are needed to confirm these findings.

cards.title: Beyond binary cGAS–STING signaling: a duration, abundance, localization, and cell type (DALT) framework for interpreting divergent findings in senescence and inflammaging
cards.abstract: Activation of cGAS–STING by aberrantly localized self-DNA is widely regarded as a mechanism linking cellular damage, senescence and age-associated inflammation. Yet the evidence no longer supports an exclusively linear interpretation in which self-DNA exposure necessarily produces cGAS activation, cGAMP synthesis, STING activation and inflammaging. DNA presence and even cGAS recruitment need not yield productive catalysis; cGAS performs nuclear functions uncoupled from cGAMP synthesis; cGAMP and immunogenic DNA itself can propagate between cells; and STING participates in translational stress responses, non-canonical autophagy, endolysosomal homeostasis and ion transport that exceed the TBK1–IRF3 axis. Interventions targeting different components during aging have produced opposing outcomes, including studies in which acute inhibition is beneficial while constitutive loss is deleterious, and studies in which the same gene exerts opposite effects in human and murine cells. Here we critically examine these divergences and propose the DALT framework—duration, abundance, localization and cell type—as a structure for interpreting the context dependence of cGAS, cGAMP and STING function. DALT does not assert that context matters, which is uncontroversial; it specifies which contextual variables must be measured and reported to facilitate meaningful comparisons across studies, and it addresses a defined problem: results currently read as contradictory frequently represent distinct configurations of the same machinery that have never been compared along the same dimensions. We give each dimension an operational definition, a measurable variable and a falsifiable prediction, apply the framework to three specific controversies, and state its limitations. The resulting question is not whether cGAS–STING is active, but how much, for how long, where, and in which cell.

cards.title: A replaceable soma enables negative senescence in harvester ants.
cards.abstract: Most vertebrates and insects undergo senescence: as they age, their rate of mortality increases while reproduction declines. We present data from a 34-y study on 3,285 colonies of known age in the western harvester ant, Pogonomyrmex occidentalis, that show the reverse pattern, negative senescence, in which mortality decreases and reproduction increases with age. Theoretical models have identified indeterminate growth and a lack of reproductive cost to growth as the key traits favoring the evolution of negative senescence. Ant colonies continue to grow throughout their lifetime, leading to older colonies being larger on average. We found no evidence of a tradeoff between colony growth and reproduction: growth and reproduction were positively correlated, a synergism that may favor continued investment in growth. Harvester ants occupy a temporally variable environment that shapes investment in reproduction. At the population level, greater reproduction in 1 y does not lead to higher numbers of new colonies in the following year. Environmental unpredictability decouples reproduction from recruitment and selects for an extended reproductive lifespan, a trait that parallels changes in aging. We discuss the features that harvester ant colonies share with other organisms to identify functionally homologous mechanisms for avoiding senescence, as well as those traits that are specific to highly eusocial species.

cards.title: A metaheuristic-based ensemble framework for osteoporosis classification using knee X-ray images.
cards.abstract: Osteoporosis is a progressive skeletal disorder characterized by reduced bone strength and increased fracture susceptibility, while its early identification from conventional radiographic images remains challenging because clinically relevant structural and textural variations can be subtle. This study proposes OsteoEnsembleNet, an ensemble stacking machine learning framework for automated osteoporosis classification using knee radiographs. The framework employs an Adaptive Unscented Kalman Filter (AUKF) for adaptive image quality enhancement, followed by a Hybrid Improved Beluga Whale Optimizer-Modified Fuzzy C-Means (HiBWmFCM) method for knee region segmentation. Multiple complementary feature domains, including morphological, statistical, gray-level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM), texture, and local binary pattern (LBP) descriptors, are subsequently extracted and optimized using HRSWaO feature selection. To improve classification robustness, predictions from seven heterogeneous classifiers-artificial neural network (ANN), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), gradient boosting, XGBoost, and AdaBoost-are integrated through a logistic regression-based stacking meta-classifier. Experiments were conducted on publicly available Knee X-ray Osteoporosis Database. On the 80:20 patient-level split, the proposed framework achieved 97.92% accuracy, 98.96% precision, 96.67% recall, 97.72% F1-score, 96.01% MCC, and 95.63% Jaccard index, with a Hamming loss of 2.08%. The results demonstrate that combining adaptive preprocessing, targeted segmentation, complementary radiographic feature representation, feature selection, and heterogeneous ensemble learning can provide consistent discrimination among Normal, Osteopenia, and Osteoporosis categories from knee X-ray images. The framework is intended as an automated image-based decision-support approach and does not directly replace quantitative bone density assessment.

cards.title: [From a broken shock absorber to robot-assisted TKA : Two-stage conversion for fracture and metallosis of a subcutaneous unloading system].
cards.abstract: A KineSpring® system (an extra-articular medial shock absorber) failed after 10 years with ring fracture and local metallosis in a 70-year-old obese patient with diabetes. Because of the infection risk, conversion was two-staged: removal, then robot-assisted TKA after 6.5 months, planned on a metal-free CT. At 12 months the patient is nearly pain-free (KOOS Pain 97.2; baseline 41.7). To our knowledge, a robot-assisted conversion has not been described before.

cards.title: Osmotic niche changes as multifaceted trigger of cellular regenerative processes in organ injury
cards.abstract: Tissue compartments can maintain distinct osmotic environments that are separated by physical barriers. Whether injury-induced osmotic niche changes associated with the disruption of these barriers contribute to the onset of regeneration remains unknown. Here we present analyses of human tissue samples indicating that fracture-induced barrier disruption likely exposes the marrow niche to a sudden hypo-osmotic shift, which enhances extracellular matrix (ECM) stress relaxation. We reveal that this hypo-osmolar shift, mimicked in vitro by lowering ion concentrations, triggers bone regenerative processes in mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs), markedly increasing their spreading, proliferation, and osteogenic differentiation while residing in osmolality-responsive viscoelastic ECM. In elastic ECM, elevated ion concentrations instead promoted osteogenic differentiation, indicating that ECM viscous dissipation redirects how cells interpret osmotic changes. Mechanistically, the regenerative function of the osmolality drop depends on the matrix providing cell-adhesion ligands and physiological viscoelastic properties. Within eight hours, hypo-osmolality amplifies pro-inflammatory and pro-angiogenic cytokine secretion (CXCL1, CCL2, CCL5, and IL-6). Within two hours, transcriptomic analyses reveal chromatin remodeling signatures specifically associated with hypo-osmolality. Within minutes, the osmolality drop alters nuclear morphology, mechanics, and chromatin organization, preceding increased osteogenic transcription factor expression. These findings identify osmotic niche disruption as a fast-acting physical signal that coordinates ECM mechanics and nuclear organization to initiate regenerative programs after injury. This osmotic stimulus may coordinate regenerative responses beyond the stromal compartment through inflammatory signaling. Leveraging osmotic cues to induce regenerative cascades may eventually advance local and personalized therapeutic strategies for patients with impaired healing capacity. The integration of osmotic and mechanical ECM properties, as demonstrated in our assay, may catalyze advanced 3D cell culture systems and offer new perspectives on material design in tissue engineering, disease modeling, and mechanobiology.

cards.title: Safety and Clinical Impact of Emergency Department Closed Reduction for Gartland Type III Supracondylar Humerus Fractures.
cards.abstract: Pediatric type 3 supracondylar humerus fractures (SCHFs) are typically immobilized in situ before definitive operative fixation because of concern for neurovascular injury during closed reduction. This study assesses the safety and clinical outcomes of emergency department (ED) closed reduction versus in situ splinting for type 3 SCHFs before definitive fixation. A retrospective review was conducted of all pediatric extension-type 3 SCHFs that underwent closed reduction versus no reduction by orthopaedic surgery residents in the ED at a single Level 1 trauma center over a 5-year period. Data included pre- and postreduction neurovascular examinations, multiple radiographic parameters, durations of time between injury, consult, and reduction to the operating room (OR), total operative time, and OR fluoroscopy duration. Of 112 patients, 54 underwent closed reduction (CR) while 58 were not reduced (NR). Nine (20%) patients in the CR group and 9 (18%) patients in the NR group had abnormal neurological exams on presentation. Four (8%) patients in the CR group and 2 (4%) patients in the NR group had abnormal vascular exams. All 4 patients who underwent closed reduction had improved vascular exams from Doppler-able to palpable radial pulses (P=0.12). No vascular injuries occurred with closed reduction. Importantly, 6 patients in the NR group with initial normal exams developed abnormal neurological deficits while awaiting surgical fixation (P=0.03). The CR group demonstrated significantly improved radiographic parameters postreduction, including AP and lateral displacement, anterior humeral line displacement, lateral Baumann angle, and hourglass angle. The time from consult or reduction to OR was significantly less for the NR group compared with the CR group (9.83 vs. 13.45 h; P<0.01). The time from injury to the OR was also significantly less in the NR group (21.0 vs. 17.0 h; P=0.02). The CR group trended towards shorter operative times (33 vs. 40 min; P=0.15). Closed reduction of pediatric type 3 SCHFs in the ED by orthopaedic surgery residents is safe and can improve both neurovascular deficits and radiographic fracture alignment. As most pediatric extremity fractures undergo closed reduction in the ED, type 3 SCHFs should not be considered an exception. Level III-retrospective comparative study.

cards.title: [German-Speaking Society for Reconstructive Microsurgery (GSRM) Consensus Statement:Orthoplastic Surgery for Primary Reconstruction of Complex Extremity Injuries -Timing, Strategy, and Technical Aspects].
cards.abstract: The goal of acute orthoplastic care is to ensure functional limb salvage through stable bony fixation and soft-tissue reconstruction. Despite the reported benefits of early interdisciplinary planning and treatment, structural deficits and the limited availability of microsurgical expertise in the DACH region (Germany, Austria, Switzerland) continue to hinder patient care. At its 46th annual meeting in November 2025, an expert panel of the GSRM analyzed procedural limitations and formulated cross-disciplinary recommendations to optimize acute orthoplastic care. In a two-step process, the committee of 132 experts first defined five core questions regarding patient navigation and centralization, quality assurance of interdisciplinary debridements, the establishment of interdisciplinary limb boards, timeframes for bony and soft-tissue reconstruction, and the interval between osteosynthesis and flap-based reconstruction. Subsequently, five corresponding consensus recommendations were unanimously adopted. The five consensus recommendations include directed navigation of patients to designated centers with sufficient expertise and interdisciplinary team meetings, the a priori interdisciplinary nature of debridements, and the earliest possible definitive management of open fractures within a maximum of 10 days - whereby osteosynthesis and soft-tissue reconstruction should be achieved in a single- or delayed single-stage procedure within 24 hours. 1. Primary care of open limb fractures in supra-regional trauma centers with 24/7 availability of plastic-reconstructive, microsurgical, and vascular surgical expertise. 2. A priori interdisciplinary initial debridements of open limb fractures involving a plastic surgeon, at the latest before definitive osteosynthesis. 3. Establishment of interdisciplinary limb boards for the collaborative development and definition of interdisciplinary treatment plans. 4. Earliest possible definitive management of open limb fractures via fixation and coverage, no later than 10 days post-injury. 5. Immediate or delayed single-stage execution of both soft-tissue reconstruction and definitive osteosynthesis within a maximum of 24 hours.

cards.title: Adverse event reporting patterns for endodontic files in the FDA MAUDE database: a postmarket surveillance analysis, 2015-2025.
cards.abstract: Endodontic files have not been specifically characterized in the FDA Manufacturer and User Facility Device Experience (MAUDE) database. We characterized adverse-event reporting patterns for heat-treated NiTi (HT), conventional austenitic NiTi (CONV) and manual hand files from 2015-2025 and evaluated whether MAUDE can support alloy-level clinical-risk inference. MAUDE reports filed from 01 January 2015 to 31 December 2025 for File, Pulp Canal, Endodontic were retrieved through the openFDA API and classified a priori by brand into HT, CONV and HAND. Groups were compared using χ2/Fisher-Freeman-Halton tests, Cramér's V, Reporting Odds Ratios (RORs) and shrinkage observed-to-expected Information Components with Gamma lower limits (IC025). A Break-excluded separation/fracture composite was the key secondary endpoint. Of 2,824 retrieved reports, 2,666 were analysed. HAND reports showed more injury events than HT reports (9.8% vs 3.0%; p < 0.001; Cramér's V = 0.112). Because HAND reports were almost entirely stainless-steel hand files (297/307, 96.7%), this represents a stainless-steel hand-file reporting signal rather than a manual-instrumentation signal. The Break-excluded composite supported this signal (ROR 3.04; IC025 0.55). A borderline Modern HT-M-Wire Material Separation contrast was not supported by Bayesian shrinkage. cards.title: Disruption of CTCF-mediated IGF2 repression promotes AKT-dependent mitochondrial oxidative stress and chondrocyte senescence in osteoarthritis.
cards.abstract: The upstream epigenetic mechanisms linking chronic inflammation to mitochondrial dysregulation and chondrocyte senescence in osteoarthritis (OA) remain incompletely defined. This study investigated whether inflammation-associated loss of CTCF occupancy at the IGF2-H19 intergenic region contributes to IGF2 upregulation, AKT-dependent mitochondrial oxidative stress, and chondrocyte senescence. Integrative transcriptomic analysis of GSE114007 was performed using DESeq2, WGCNA, and protein-protein interaction network analysis. Key findings were examined in human OA cartilage and mechanistically investigated in cytokine-stimulated C28/I2 chondrocytes using chromatin immunoprecipitation, mitochondrial functional profiling, and senescence assays. Mechanistic studies combined CTCF gain- and loss-of-function approaches with pharmacological targeting of IGF2, AKT, and mitochondrial ROS. IGF2 neutralization was further evaluated in an ACLT murine model. IGF2 emerged as a transcriptomic hub gene associated with mitochondrial and senescence-related networks in OA. Inflammatory stimulation reduced CTCF expression and occupancy at the IGF2-H19 intergenic region, accompanied by increased IGF2 expression, AKT activation, mitochondrial respiratory activity, ROS production, matrix catabolism, and senescence-associated phenotypes. CTCF overexpression attenuated IGF2 upregulation and oxidative/senescence-associated phenotypes, whereas CTCF knockdown elicited complementary changes. Targeting IGF2, AKT, or mitochondrial ROS reduced oxidative stress and senescence-associated changes. In vivo, IGF2 neutralization attenuated cartilage degeneration, matrix catabolism, AKT activation, and senescence-associated alterations. These findings support a functional regulatory framework linking CTCF-IGF2 dysregulation with AKT-dependent mitochondrial oxidative stress and chondrocyte senescence in OA, highlighting IGF2 signaling as a potential therapeutic target.

cards.title: Cuproptosis in age-related orthopedic diseases: mechanisms and therapeutic prospects.
cards.abstract: Cuproptosis is an emerging copper-dependent and mitochondria-associated form of regulated cell death (RCD) that links intracellular labile copper accumulation to metabolic vulnerability. Mechanistically, cuproptosis is triggered by intracellular copper accumulation, leading to aggregation of lipoylated tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle proteins, destabilization of iron-sulfur cluster proteins, and proteotoxic stress-induced bioenergetic collapse. Aging-associated orthopedic disorders-including osteoarthritis (OA), osteoporosis (OP) and intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD)-represent a rapidly expanding global burden and share convergent pathological features such as mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, chronic low-grade inflammation, and progressive skeletal cell loss. However, the upstream regulatory networks integrating these hallmarks remain incompletely defined. Aging may be accompanied by systemic copper redistribution, impaired intracellular copper buffering, expansion of labile copper pools in vulnerable cellular microenvironments, and concomitant iron dysregulation. Together, these alterations form an interconnected metal-redox-metabolic axis that sensitizes skeletal tissues to degenerative remodeling. In this review, we synthesize current advances in copper homeostasis and the molecular determinants of cuproptosis, with particular emphasis on their potential involvement in OA, OP, and IVDD. We further distinguish established evidence from mechanistic hypotheses and discuss why serum copper, tissue copper, and intracellular labile copper should not be interpreted interchangeably. Finally, we outline future perspectives on targeting cuproptosis for the treatment of age-related orthopedic diseases, aiming to stimulate further clinical investigation and therapeutic innovation.

cards.title: Targeting the AKT2-NAMPT phosphorylation axis prevents macrophage senescence to enhance bactericidal activity in septic immunosuppression.
cards.abstract: Macrophage immune dysregulation in sepsis contributes to secondary infections and poor outcomes. Immunosuppression, a key feature of this dysregulation, has been linked to the acquisition of cellular senescence-like features in cancer. However, the mechanistic connection between immune tolerance, a well-established cellular model of immunosuppression, and macrophage senescence remains poorly understood. Here, using an in vitro model of lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced tolerance, we found that immune-tolerant macrophages acquired a senescent phenotype. Unexpectedly, nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT) mRNA and protein levels were markedly upregulated in tolerant macrophages despite profound suppression of MYC proto-oncogene (MYC), a canonical transcriptional regulator of NAMPT. Mechanistically, this paradoxical accumulation of NAMPT was driven by reduced expression of the RNA helicase DEAD-box helicase 6 (DDX6), thereby enhancing NAMPT mRNA stability. However, increased NAMPT abundance was uncoupled from its enzymatic activity owing to diminished AKT serine/threonine kinase 2 (AKT2)-mediated phosphorylation. Treatment with SC79, a pan-AKT activator, restored NAMPT phosphorylation and activity, attenuated senescence-associated markers, and enhanced bactericidal function in tolerant macrophages. In a murine model of sepsis, alveolar macrophages similarly exhibited reduced DDX6 and AKT2 expression, together with elevated NAMPT abundance, corroborating the in vitro findings. Collectively, these results identify a dual-layer regulatory mechanism in which DDX6 controls NAMPT abundance, whereas AKT2 dictates its activity. The uncoupling of NAMPT abundance from its enzymatic activity drives senescence during immune tolerance, identifying AKT2-NAMPT as a potential therapeutic axis to restore immune competence in sepsis.

cards.title: Circulating C-Terminal Agrin Fragment is Associated with Impaired Physical Performance in Aging and Chronic Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
cards.abstract: Circulating C-terminal agrin fragment (CAF22) is a biomarker of neuromuscular junction degradation and sarcopenia. However, its relationship with objective measures of physical performance has not been systematically evaluated. This systematic review and meta-analysis examined associations of circulating CAF22 concentrations with gait speed and Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) scores in aging and chronic disease populations. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar were searched to identify studies reporting associations between circulating CAF22 concentrations and gait speed and/or SPPB scores. Correlation coefficients were extracted, transformed to Fisher's z values, and pooled using random-effects meta-analysis. Risk of bias, heterogeneity, subgroup differences, and publication bias were assessed. Twenty-one studies met the inclusion criteria, contributing 33 cohorts for gait speed (n = 3136) and 28 cohorts for SPPB (n = 2773). Higher circulating CAF22 concentrations were significantly associated with slower gait speed in controls (r = - 0.309, 95% CI - 0.371 to - 0.244%) and disease cohorts (r = - 0.309, 95% CI - 0.361 to - 0.254%), yielding an overall pooled correlation of r = - 0.308 (95% CI - 0.346 to - 0.269%). CAF22 concentrations were also inversely associated with SPPB scores in controls (r = - 0.335, 95% CI - 0.415 to - 0.250%) and disease cohorts (r = - 0.368, 95% CI - 0.422 to - 0.312%), with an overall pooled correlation of r = - 0.353 (95% CI - 0.397 to - 0.307%). No significant subgroup differences were detected. Elevated circulating CAF22 concentrations are consistently associated with poorer physical performance across healthy and chronic disease populations, supporting CAF22 as a promising biomarker of functional decline.

cards.title: Estimated glucose disposal rate is inversely associated with frailty and cardiovascular mortality: Evidence from NHANES 2001 to 2018.
cards.abstract: With global population aging, the prevalence of frailty is steadily increasing. Insulin resistance plays a key role in the development of frailty and cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality. The estimated glucose disposal rate (eGDR) has been recognized as a reliable surrogate marker of insulin resistance. To date, no studies have investigated the association between eGDR, frailty, and CVD mortality in the U.S. population. We used data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2001 to 2018 cycles and employed weighted logistic regression and weighted Cox proportional hazards models to evaluate the associations between eGDR and frailty, as well as CVD mortality among frail and non-frail individuals. Restricted cubic spline analysis was used to explore potential nonlinear relationships, and subgroup analyses were conducted to test the robustness of the findings. The results indicated a significant inverse association between eGDR and frailty prevalence; each 1 standard deviation increase in eGDR was associated with a 22.3% decrease in frailty risk (odds ratio = 0.777 [0.760, 0.795]). Higher eGDR levels were also significantly associated with lower CVD mortality risk. Among frail individuals, each standard deviation increase in eGDR was associated with a 4.3% lower risk of CVD mortality (hazard ratio = 0.957 [0.916, 0.988]); among non-frail individuals, the corresponding reduction was 7% (hazard ratio = 0.930 [0.885, 0.977]). The inverse association showed a stronger gradient across eGDR levels among non-frail individuals, whereas this pattern was not observed among frail individuals. Restricted cubic spline analysis revealed a nonlinear association between eGDR and both frailty and CVD mortality among frail individuals, whereas a linear relationship was observed among non-frail individuals. Subgroup analysis indicated that age modified the associations between eGDR, frailty, and CVD mortality in frail individuals. Smoking status influenced the relationship between eGDR and frailty, while race modified the association between eGDR and CVD mortality among non-frail individuals. eGDR was significantly and inversely associated with frailty and CVD mortality in both frail and non-frail populations. Higher eGDR levels were associated with a lower prevalence of frailty and lower cardiovascular mortality risk, suggesting that eGDR may serve as a potential marker for metabolic and cardiovascular risk stratification.

cards.title: Rejuvenation rankings from CRISPRi screens change with the aging cohort and track cell growth programs
cards.abstract: Ranking gene knockdowns by how well they reverse an aging expression signature is a common way to find rejuvenation targets, but the stability of these rankings has not been tested. We built TRACE, an open-source set of tests, to score 18,746 knockdown profiles from five CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) screens in four human cell lines. Rankings built from fibroblasts of 111 donors and from Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) fibroblasts were unrelated (ρ = −0.05). In an exploratory test, the 200 strongest age genes of the first cohort changed in the opposite direction in GTEx (ρ = −0.55), but this was not significant after correction and shrank when GTEx batch was modeled. Raw scores followed the broad programs inside each signature: strongly for proliferation with the fibroblast signature, weakly for stress with a GTEx-derived signature. Proliferation alone matched the fibroblast scores' agreement with senescence labels. TRACE runs on other aging cohorts and screens.

cards.title: Sclerostin actions in bone and metabolic disease.
cards.abstract: Sclerostin, a 24 kDa glycoprotein secreted primarily by matrix-embedded osteocytes, plays an essential role in the maintenance of bone mass. Sclerostin acts as a suppressor of bone mass accrual through its inhibitory effects on Wnt/β-catenin signaling, which is most dramatically observed in the rare bone overgrowth conditions associated with SOST gene loss of function in humans and laboratory models. In recent years, a second extra-skeletal function for sclerostin has emerged due to its presence in the circulation and the association between serum levels and metabolic indices. Indeed, genetic and pharmacologic inhibition of sclerostin reduces the accumulation of adipose tissue mass and improves insulin sensitivity in mouse models. In this review, we provide an overview of both the basic science and clinical studies that serve as a rationale for the targeting of sclerostin in the treatment of bone loss and describe pre-clinical research focused on sclerostin's actions as a bone-derived endocrine factor that contributes to the skeleton's influence on systemic metabolism and integrative physiology.

cards.title: Psychometric validation of the European Portuguese version of Quality of Life Questionnaire of the European Foundation for Osteoporosis (QUALEFFO-41) in the Portuguese population.
cards.abstract: The European Portuguese version of the QUALEFFO-41 showed good reliability, validity, and excellent discriminatory ability between patients with vertebral fragility fractures and controls. These findings support its use as a disease-specific quality-of-life instrument in Portuguese clinical practice and research. Vertebral fragility fractures substantially impair quality of life (QoL). The Quality of Life Questionnaire of the European Foundation for Osteoporosis (QUALEFFO-41) is a disease-specific instrument widely used to assess QoL in patients with vertebral fractures; however, its psychometric properties have not yet been validated for use in Portugal. This study aimed to perform the psychometric validation of the European Portuguese version of the QUALEFFO-41. A multicentric prospective validation study was conducted in Portuguese patients with vertebral fragility fractures and age- and sex-matched controls. Following cognitive debriefing and cultural adaptation, participants completed the QUALEFFO-41 and the SF-36, with a 2-week retest interval. Internal consistency (Cronbach's α), test-retest reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient, ICC), construct validity (convergent and discriminant validity), criterion validity (correlations with SF-36), and discriminatory ability were assessed. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses were performed to determine optimal cut-off points. Seventy-five participants were included (55 patients with vertebral fragility fractures and 20 controls). Internal consistency was adequate across domains (Cronbach's α 0.70-0.98) and excellent for the total score (α = 0.90). Test-retest reliability was high, with ICCs ranging from 0.75 to 0.98. Multitrait analysis demonstrated satisfactory convergent (71.4-100%) and discriminant validity (70.6-100%). Significant correlations were observed between QUALEFFO-41 domains and corresponding SF-36 domains, particularly for general health perception (r = -0.85). Patients with vertebral fragility fractures reported significantly worse QoL than controls across all domains and the total score (p < 0.001), with large effect sizes (Cohen's d 0.93-1.90). ROC analyses showed good to excellent discriminatory performance (AUC 0.75-0.92). The European Portuguese version of the QUALEFFO-41 demonstrates robust reliability, validity, and strong discriminatory capacity. It is a valid and reliable instrument for assessing quality of life in Portuguese patients with vertebral fragility fractures in both clinical practice and research settings.

cards.title: A pilot study on the impact of Hydroxiram D supplementation on nutritional status and sarcopenia-related parameters.
cards.abstract: Sarcopenia is a frequent and prognostically relevant complication of chronic liver disease. The SARCIRAM pilot trial investigated the effect of Hydroxiram D, a formulation of branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs), β-hydroxy-β-methylbutyrate (HMB), and vitamin D, on nutritional status and sarcopenia-related parameters in patients with compensated cirrhosis due to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). In this single-center, randomized pilot study, adults with compensated MASLD-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A) received Hydroxiram D plus standard care or standard care alone for 6 months. The primary outcome was phase angle (PA), while secondary outcomes were appendicular skeletal muscle mass (ASMM)/height², handgrip strength (HGS), and 4-meter walk test (4-mWT). Between-group comparisons used baseline-adjusted models. Post-hoc simulation analyses were used exploratorily to inform the design of future studies. Thirty-two patients were analyzed. After 6 months, the adjusted change in PA was significantly more favorable in the treated group versus controls (+ 0.36° vs. - 0.45°, p = 0.046). Between-group differences in muscle mass, HGS, and gait speed were not statistically significant, although effect estimates directionally favoured the intervention. No treatment-related adverse events were observed. Six months of Hydroxiram D was associated with a more favorable change in PA in patients with compensated MASLD-related cirrhosis, with favorable trends in muscle parameters. These hypothesis-generating findings warrant confirmation in larger, prospectively registered, double-blind trials to confirm efficacy and long-term outcomes.

cards.title: HOW SAFE IS EXERCISE? CROSS-SECTIONAL ASSOCIATIONS OF CURRENT PHYSICAL ACTIVITY WITH SELF-REPORTED FRACTURE HISTORY IN MID-LIFE
cards.abstract: ObjectiveTo examine associations between the volume and intensity of leisure-time physical activity (LTPA) and fracture during mid-life, and whether adherence to World Health Organization (WHO) physical activity recommendations was associated with fracture. MethodsCross-sectional analysis of 322,749 UK Biobank participants aged 40-65 years using self-reported physical activity and fracture data. LTPA volume (LTPAv) was derived from walking, moderate and vigorous activity. Participants were categorised into LTPAv quintiles and by adherence to WHO physical activity recommendations. Multivariable logistic regression examined associations with self-reported fracture within the previous five years, with analyses stratified by sex and adjusted for sociodemographic and anthropometric factors. Walking, moderate and vigorous activity were mutually adjusted to examine associations by intensity. ResultsParticipants had a mean age of 47 years and 53% were female. Odds of fracture increased with higher LTPAv, although associations were non-linear and varied by age and sex. Associations were strongest in the highest quintile among men and women aged 40-49 years (OR 1.81, 95% CI 1.64-1.99 and OR 1.42, 95% CI 1.28-1.58, respectively). Vigorous activity demonstrated the strongest independent association with fracture. Meeting, without exceeding, WHO physical activity recommendations was not associated with increased odds of fracture. ConclusionsHigher LTPA volumes were associated with greater odds of fracture, particularly vigorous activity, with associations strongest in younger adults and men. Activity consistent with WHO recommendations was not associated with greater odds of fracture, supporting continued promotion of physical activity during mid-life.

cards.title: How the aging immune system fuels neurodegeneration: the role of immune cell exhaustion and immunosenescence
cards.abstract: Abstract Age-related neurodegenerative diseases (ARNDs), including Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and Parkinson’s disease (PD), are increasingly recognized as disorders involving systemic immune dysfunction in addition to central nervous system pathology. While chronic neuroinflammation is a well-established hallmark of both diseases, emerging evidence suggests that aging and chronic systemic inflammation may ultimately drive immune cell exhaustion and immunosenescence, which may in turn impair immune surveillance and protein clearance, contributing to progressive neurodegeneration. Here, we review clinical and preclinical evidence supporting exhaustion- and senescence-associated phenotypes across peripheral and central immune compartments in AD and PD. We first outline the spectrum of immune activation states and describe how aging and chronic systemic inflammation remodel immune function toward exhausted and senescent states. We then examine evidence linking these processes to disease progression, highlighting mechanisms involving impaired adaptive and innate immune responses, metabolic dysfunction, and neuroimmune crosstalk. Finally, we contrast these findings with observations from cognitively healthy centenarians, whose preserved immune competence suggests that maintenance of immune fitness may promote resilience against neurodegeneration. Collectively, the available evidence supports a conceptual shift from viewing ARNDs solely as diseases of excessive inflammation toward recognizing progressive loss of immunocompetence as a key contributor to pathogenesis, with important implications for the development of therapies that restore, rather than suppress, immune function.

cards.title: Reprogramming transcription factor networks with a HOX inhibitor to address Huntington's disease biology beyond mutant huntingtin
cards.abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is an inherited neurodegenerative disorder caused by CAG-repeat expansion in the huntingtin (HTT) gene. Although inherited CAG-repeat length and the underlying somatic instability are key determinants of age at onset, they explain only part of onset variability, suggesting additional disease mechanisms. We applied the Core Coefficient (CC), a transcription-factor (TF) network-decoding technology that quantifies TF functional dominance, to >100 post-mortem neuronal transcriptomes from HD and control brain datasets. Among human TF families, the HOX family is the only family that uniformly exhibits quiescence in controls versus large and significant functional dominance in vulnerable neurons of each HD donor brain we investigated. HOX TFs are already dominant at Vonsattel grade 0 and at inherited CAG-repeat length. The magnitude of HOX CC values correlates with age at onset and increases with disease grade and CAG-Age Product. HOX TFs form a self-sustained pathological unit targeting >4,000 genes implicated in neuronal patterning, identity, stress, signaling, structure, and senescence. In zQ175 mice, abrogation of mutant huntingtin (mHTT) protein production only transiently attenuates HOX dominance and does not durably eliminate it. COR-H800, a HOX inhibitor, restored TF-network hierarchy toward wild type, normalizing the functional dominance of transcription factors involved in neuronal differentiation, cell-fate determination, and developmental patterning, and improved disease-relevant phenotypes in R6/2 mice. These findings support the direct selective inhibition of HOX TFs to address the aberrant transcriptional state that can persist despite mHTT lowering or somatic instability-targeted therapeutic interventions.

cards.title: [Dual plate fixation in complex distal femoral metaphyseal fractures].
cards.abstract: Distal femur fractures are rare injuries and show a bimodal distribution pattern: firstly, young patients following high-energy trauma, and secondly, geriatric patients. Simple fractures can be treated with intramedullary nailing or plate osteosynthesis, while double plate osteosynthesis is useful for more complex fractures to improve fracture stability and promote healing. Stable, osteosynthetic procedure for multifragmentary distal femoral fractures with optimal preservation of physiology. Complex, distal femoral fractures with multifragmentary, metaphyseal components. Major soft tissue defects, general condition of the patient not permitting treatment, bedridden status. Double plate osteosynthesis of the distal femur via a lateral approach and a medial subvastus approach. Following surgery, 15 kg partial weight-bearing on the operated leg with forearm crutches for 6 weeks. In geriatric patients, pain-adapted full weight-bearing to avoid secondary complications. Retrospective evaluation of cases from January 2020 to September 2024 revealed complications in 2 of 11 patients who underwent surgery; 1 patient died during the course of subsequent surgeries.

cards.title: The Influence of Long-Term Supplementation with Lactiplantibacillus plantarum LP28 on NK Cell Activity and Upper Respiratory Symptoms in Middle-Aged and Older Adults: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial
cards.abstract: Background: Population aging and immunosenescence pose immense challenges to healthcare systems by increasing susceptibility to infections. Lactiplantibacillus plantarum LP28 (L. plantarum LP28) is a strain isolated from traditional Taiwanese dried tofu with significant immunomodulatory potential. Objective: To evaluate the clinical efficacy of long-term L. plantarum LP28 supplementation in common cold prevention and its effect on systemic immune biomarkers in middle-aged and elderly individuals. Methods: In this 12-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 102 middle-aged and older adults (aged 50-75 years) were assigned to receive an oral probiotic (5 x 109 CFU L. plantarum LP28/capsule, two capsules daily; n = 51) or a placebo (n = 51). Cold incidence and symptom severity were evaluated by the Wisconsin Upper Respiratory Symptom Survey (WURSS). Immune cell populations, serum/salivary markers, and natural killer (NK) cell activity were quantified using flow cytometry, ELISAs and NK cell cytotoxicity assays, respectively. The data were analyzed using a refined per-protocol approach and outlier-removed sensitivity analyses to ensure robustness. Independent t tests, chi-square/Fisher's exact tests, and Mann-Whitney U tests were used for statistical comparisons. Results: The probiotic group exhibited a notable reduction in cold incidence (34.78% vs. 52.00% in the placebo group) and a lower cumulative symptom burden. In terms of immunomodulatory effects, L. plantarum LP28 supplementation significantly increased serum interleukin (IL)-12 levels and NK cell cytotoxicity, reinforcing innate immune defense through the activation of the IL-12/NK cell axis. This was accompanied by a significant reduction in the level of the inflammatory marker C-reactive protein (CRP). Conclusions: L. plantarum LP28 supplementation serves as an effective supportive strategy for promoting healthy aging by increasing respiratory defense resilience and mitigating systemic inflammatory stress through pleiotropic immune modulation.

cards.title: Predictors of Success in Fractured Electrode Extraction: The Impact of Fracture Location and Access Strategies.
cards.abstract: Fractured or sheared cardiac implantable electronic device leads presents a unique clinical challenge in transvenous lead extraction. These cases are associated with clinical failure rates of up to 40% and a greater likelihood of retained fragments. The aim of this study was to characterize fractured lead extractions performed at a referral center and identify predictors of complete removal and clinical success. We conducted a retrospective single center study including all consecutive patients who underwent TLE for electrodes fractured before or during extraction between October 2011 and December 2025. Clinical, echocardiographic, and procedural data were collected. A total of 46 procedures were analyzed. Mean age was 62.7 years and median lead dwell time was 9.0 years. The most frequent fracture site was the electrode body (67.4%). A rotational mechanical sheath was used in 84.8% of cases (39/46), and femoral snaring was used in 60.8%. Complete extraction occurred in 32.6% whereas clinical success was achieved in 80.4% of patients. Retained fragments > 4 cm were observed in 28.3%. In multivariate analysis, the use of a 13Fr sheath was independently associated with lower odds of clinical success (p = 0.011). Fracture location was the only consistent independent predictor of complete extraction (p = 0.031). Femoral access showed a favorable trend but did not reach statistical significance after adjustment. In fractured lead extraction, fracture location is the strongest predictor of complete removal, surpassing clinical and procedural variables. These findings highlight the importance of preoperative planning and suggest that femoral access may play a key role in selected complex cases.

cards.title: Terminal differentiation program of CD8 T cells guides immunotherapeutic options for CLL patients.
cards.abstract: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) remains incurable and autologous T-cell-based therapies induce durable remissions in only a minority of patients. Although poor T-cell performance in CLL has been attributed to exhaustion, T cells from CLL patients retain cytokine production and lack key transcriptional markers of exhaustion, suggesting an alternative state of differentiation. Here, we performed an integrated phenotypic, epigenetic and functional analysis of circulating CD8⁺ T cells from treatment-naive CLL patients to define the nature and therapeutic relevance of terminal differentiation in CLL. CD8⁺ T cells from treatment-naive CLL patients were enriched for a terminally differentiated, CD27⁻CD28⁻CD57⁺KLRG1⁺ population with several senescence-associated features, including increased cell size, granularity, β-galactosidase activity, and reduced basal autophagy. However, these cells lacked key hallmarks of irreversible senescence. Instead, CLL T cells mounted robust but transient proliferative bursts and developed activation-associated γH2AX signals followed by impaired persistence and increased cell death upon repeated activation. Especially CD57⁺ T cells were vulnerable and incompatible with the experimental steps required for CAR T-cell manufacturing. The potent, acute effector function of these cells could, however, be harnessed by bispecific T-cell engagers, which induced effective cytolysis of both cell lines and primary CLL targets by these T cells. Collectively, our data support a model in which CD8+ T-cell dysfunction in CLL reflects accumulation of short-lived, terminally differentiated effector cells rather than canonical exhaustion or irreversible senescence. This state limits durable persistence required for CAR T-cell approached while preserving acute cytotoxicity relevant for bispecific antibody-based therapies in CLL.

cards.title: International Model to Inform the Care of Individuals with a Vertebral Fragility Fracture.
cards.abstract: Vertebral fragility fractures (VFF) are associated with pain, impaired function, and increased fracture risk. Our aim was to develop an internationally applicable model to guide the care of individuals with VFF. The Fragility Fracture Network (FFN) VFF Special Interest Group established the project structure and scope: review existing guidance and adapt recommendations and a visual model; solicit knowledge user feedback; make iterative revisions to the recommendations and visual model based on feedback; and finalize the recommendations. The model adapts recommendations from a published international Delphi consensus and national guidance. Knowledge user feedback was obtained through a survey disseminated via FFN channels across 40 countries. The survey responses informed iterative revision and finalization of the care model. The final VFF care model comprised three domains. 'Pain management' emphasizes structured pain and physical functioning assessment, multimodal pharmacological and non-pharmacological strategies, patient education, and timely referral for specialist review when indicated. The domain 'Improving Physical Functioning' included promoting movement, early mobilization, exercise focused on strength, balance, and back extensor endurance, and behaviour change approaches to support return to physical activities of leisure and daily living. The domain, Fall and Fracture Prevention, integrates falls and fracture risk assessment and prevention. It included nutritional evaluation, optimization of vitamin D and calcium intake, osteoporosis medication initiation, and referral for exercise, home hazard assessment, and specialist input. Cross-cutting components included patient education, behavioural support, and communication to ensure continuity of care. The VFF care model offers a comprehensive framework adaptable to diverse settings and an international perspective. Its multidisciplinary approach addresses gaps in VFF management and includes defined Key Performance Indicators. A multidisciplinary team developed an internationally applicable model to guide the care of individuals with vertebral fragility fracture, with input from knowledge users in 40 countries, with recommendations on pain management, improving physical functioning, and preventing falls and fractures.
